title: Mock 1 · Jackson: credit models and CDS
body:
Mark Jackson is a credit portfolio manager. He is reviewing several positions in his portfolio.
Jackson holds an A-rated bond issued by Don Vallejo, a large US tequila producer. The bond has a YTM of 1.0% and a modified duration of 4.5. He computes its expected 1-year total return under a credit rating migration scenario based on the 1-year credit transition matrix in Exhibit 1 where, for example, the probability of an AAA-rated bond having an A rating at the end of the year is 3%. He also uses the expected credit spread change of an A-rated bond for each possible credit rating migration, as shown in Exhibit 2.
Exhibit 1
From/To
(Entries are in %)	AAA	AA	A	BBB	BB	B	CCC
AAA	85	4	3	2	2	2	2
AA	5	83	4	3	3	1	1
A	2	3	88	2	2	2	1
BBB	1	1	3	90	3	1	1
BB	1	1	3	4	85	4	2
B	0	0	1	2	3	87	7
CCC	0	0	0	2	5	11	82
Exhibit 2
 	AAA	AA	A	BBB	BB	B	CCC
Expected change in credit spread (in bps)	50	30	0	40	60	80	150
Next, Jackson performs a credit analysis for a commercial ABS collateralized by short-term loans to small US retailers. He notes that the loan pool is granular and homogeneous. Jackson considers three approaches for the credit analysis of the ABS: loan-by-loan, portfolio-based, or statistics-based.
Jackson owns $20 million of face value of Bond X, a bond issued by Electric Motors, Incorporated. Jackson recently bought protection using a $20 million notional value CDS on Electric Motors. Two bonds can be delivered to settle the CDS upon a credit event: Bond X and Bond Y. Electric Motors declares bankruptcy, triggering a credit event on the CDS. Upon default, Bond X trades at 40% of its face value and Bond Y trades at 35% of its face value.
Jackson expects that the CDS curve of Crispy Chips, Inc., which is currently upward sloping, will flatten in the near term. Crispy Chips CDS contracts have 1-year, 3-year, and 5-year maturities. He considers using one of the following curve strategies to profit from his expectation. He assumes equal absolute notional values for each trade in each strategy.
Strategy 1: Sell protection using the 1-year contract and buy protection using the 5-year contract.
Strategy 2: Buy protection using the 3-year contract and sell protection using the 5-year contract.
Strategy 3: Buy protection using the 1-year contract and sell protection using the 5-year contract.

questions.q: The expected 1-year total return for the Don Vallejo A-rated bond under Jackson’s credit migration scenario is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the YTM is not considered when calculating the total return of the bond. In this case, the expected 1-year total return of the bond is only equal to the expected price return from a change in the credit spread.
The expected credit spread change is the probability-weighted spread change, where the probabilities are retrieved from the transition matrix row with the label rating of "A".
We first compute the expected percentage price change using the modified duration of 4.5 for each rating migration.
From A to AAA	–4.5 × –0.5% = 2.25%
From A to AA	–4.5 × –0.3% = 1.35%
From A to A	–4.5 × 0% = 0%
From A to BBB	–4.5 × 0.4% = –1.8%
From A to BB	–4.5 × 0.6% = –2.7%
From A to B	–4.5 × 0.8% = –3.6%
From A to CCC	–4.5 × 1.5% = –6.75%
The expected price return is computed by multiplying each price change by the appropriate probability from the transition matrix in the row with the label rating of "A".
Expected price return = 2.25% × 0.02 + 1.35% × 0.03 + 0% × 0.88 – 1.8% × 0.02 – 2.7% × 0.02 – 3.6% × 0.02 – 6.75% × 0.01 
= –0.144%, which is rounded to –0.14%.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the expected total return of the A-rated bond is the sum of the YTM and the expected percentage change in bond value. The YTM is 1%, while the expected return due to a credit spread change can be computed as (minus) the expected spread change (subject to migration) times the modified duration of the bond of 4.5. In turn, the expected spread change for an A-rated bond is the probability-weighted spread change, where the probabilities are retrieved from the transition matrix row with the label rating of "A".
We first compute the expected percentage price change using the modified duration of 4.5 for each rating migration.
From A to AAA	–4.5 × –0.5% = 2.25%
From A to AA	–4.5 × –0.3% = 1.35%
From A to A	–4.5 × 0% = 0%
From A to BBB	–4.5 × 0.4% = –1.8%
From A to BB	–4.5 × 0.6% = –2.7%
From A to B	–4.5 × 0.8% = –3.6%
From A to CCC	–4.5 × 1.5% = –6.75%
The expected price return is computed by multiplying each price change by the appropriate probability from the transition matrix in the row with the label rating of "A".
Expected price return = 2.25% × 0.02 + 1.35% × 0.03 + 0% × 0.88 – 1.8% × 0.02 – 2.7% × 0.02 – 3.6% × 0.02 – 6.75% × 0.01 = –0.144%
The expected total return of the bond is therefore: –0.144% + 1% = 0.856%, which is rounded to 0.86%.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the probabilities corresponding to the "A" column rather than the "A" row are retrieved from the transition matrix. Note that in this case the probabilities do not sum to 100% as the rows (but not the columns) need to sum to 1.
We first compute the expected percentage price change using the modified duration of 4.5 for each rating migration.
From A to AAA	–4.5 × –0.5% = 2.25%
From A to AA	–4.5 × –0.3% = 1.35%
From A to A	–4.5 × 0% = 0%
From A to BBB	–4.5 × 0.4% = –1.8%
From A to BB	–4.5 × 0.6% = –2.7%
From A to B	–4.5 × 0.8% = –3.6%
From A to CCC	–4.5 × 1.5% = –6.75%
The expected price return is computed by multiplying each price change by the probability from the transition matrix in the column with the label rating of "A".
Expected price return = 2.25% × 0.03 + 1.35% × 0.04 + 0% × 0.88 – 1.8% × 0.03 – 2.7% × 0.03 – 3.6% × 0.01 – 6.75% × 0 = –0.0495%
The expected total return of the bond: –0.0495% + 1% = 0.9505%, which is rounded to 0.95%.

questions.q: The most suitable approach for the credit analysis of the commercial ABS is:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because a loan-by-loan approach is not suitable when the portfolio is granular and homogeneous. Evaluating each loan on an individual basis is too time-consuming and therefore it is not suitable in this case. A loan-by-loan approach would be inefficient because of the large number of basically similar loans.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because a portfolio-based approach is not suitable when the portfolio of loans is short-term, as the portfolio does not materially change in the short term. Short-term structured finance vehicles with granular, homogeneous assets tend to be evaluated using a statistics-based approach to the existing book of loans. A portfolio-based approach is instead more suitable when the portfolio of loans is medium-term/dynamic and therefore subject to change over time.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because short-term structured finance vehicles with granular, homogeneous assets tend to be evaluated using a statistics-based approach to the existing book of loans. A statistics-based approach is most suitable when the portfolio of loans is short-term (and therefore fairly static), granular, and homogeneous, like in this case. Portfolio statistics are sufficient to appropriately analyze the credit of the loan pool.

questions.q: At settlement of the Electric Motors CDS, the total proceeds from Jackson’s Bond X and CDS positions are:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because one may:
conclude that the cheapest-to-deliver bond is Bond X, as Jackson buys protection using a CDS contract in order to protect from a credit event, and
incorrectly use the recovery rate of Bond Y to value the position in Bond X.
In this case, upon default the value of the position is computed as follows:
The position on Bond X is valued $20 million × 35% = $7 million.
The payoff on the CDS contract is $20 million × 60% = $12 million.
The total proceeds from the combined position are therefore $7 million + $12 million = $19 million.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because one may conclude that the cheapest-to-deliver bond is Bond X, as Jackson buys protection using a CDS contract in order to protect from a credit event.
In this case, upon default the value of the position is computed as follows:
The position on Bond X is valued $20 million × 40% = $8 million.
The payoff on the CDS contract is $20 million × 60% = $12 million.
The total proceeds from the combined position are therefore $8 million + $12 million = $20 million.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because Jackson holds a $20 million position in Bond X, and simultaneously has bought protection using a CDS contract referencing Electric Motors.
Upon default, the value of the position is computed as follows:
The position on Bond X is valued $20 million × 40% = $8 million.
The payoff on the CDS contract is $20 million × 65% = $13 million.
The cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) contract is the one which shall be chosen to deliver. As Bond Y trades at 35% of face value while Bond X trades at 40% of face value, Bond Y is the CTD contract and therefore the recovery rate of the CDS contract is 65%.
The total proceeds from the combined position are therefore $8 million + $13 million = $21 million.

questions.q: Which of the following strategies should profit the most from the expected flattening of the Crispy Chips CDS curve?
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because, as the Crispy Chips CDS curve is expected to flatten, Jackson should sell protection using the 5-year contract in order to maximize the gains from a tightening of long-term CDS spreads. On the contrary, buying protection using the 1-year contract minimizes the losses from widening of short-term CDS spreads.
Strategy 1 incorrectly suggests that selling protection is profitable when CDS spreads increase (rather than decrease), and conversely that buying protection is profitable when CDS spreads decrease (rather than increase). 

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because, as the Crispy Chips CDS curve is expected to flatten, Jackson should sell protection using the 5-year contract in order to maximize the gains from a tightening of long-term CDS spreads. On the contrary, buying protection using the 3-year contract is not the best strategy—losses are minimized when Jackson buys protection using the 1-year contract rather than the 3-year contract.
Strategy 2 is not the one which Jackson should implement, as Strategy 3 is more profitable. 

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because, as the Crispy Chips CDS curve is expected to flatten, Jackson should sell protection using the 5-year contract in order to maximize the gains from a tightening of long-term CDS spreads. On the contrary, buying protection using the 1-year contract minimizes the losses from widening of short-term CDS spreads.
Put differently, protection at the short end is expected to become more expensive, so he should buy it now, while protection at the long end is becoming cheaper, so he should sell it now.
Strategy 3 is the one which Jackson should implement as it yields the maximum profit, should Jackson's expected flattening of the CDS curve materialize.

title: Mock 1 · Romano: Celeste S.A. foreign currency
body:
Serrana Romano is a financial analyst reviewing Celeste S.A., a Uruguayan corporation. Celeste reports under IFRS, its reporting currency is the Uruguayan Peso (UYU), and its financial year end is 31 December.
Romano uses the following UYU/USD (number of UYU per 1 USD) exchange rate information for the most recent year.
Exhibit 1
Date	Exchange Rate UYU/USD
1 January	41.88
15 November	42.95
31 December	44.63
Average for the year	43.26
On 15 November of the most recent year, Celeste exported goods for USD 5 million to an unaffiliated US customer on credit. The total amount remained outstanding as of 31 December.
Salto Corp. and Monte Corp. are two wholly owned subsidiaries of Celeste that are located in the US. There are no intercompany transactions. In both subsidiaries, the only non-monetary assets are inventory and fixed assets, and all liabilities are monetary.
Celeste translates Salto’s financial statements using the current rate method. In the most recent year, Salto’s revenue was USD 120 million and cost of sales was USD 65 million. The average exchange rate for inventory purchases was 42.81 UYU/USD.
Celeste uses the temporal method to translate Monte’s financial statements. Romano evaluates the effect on Celeste’s total shareholders’ equity if Monte’s financial statements had been translated using the same method as Salto. The average exchange rate for both inventory and fixed assets purchases was 42.15 UYU/USD.
Celeste has recently acquired a new subsidiary that operates in a country with a highly inflationary economy. In compliance with IFRS, the subsidiary prepares financial statements restated for inflation in the local currency. At the end of the current reporting period, Celeste will prepare consolidated financial statements using the new subsidiary’s financial statements, and translate them using the exchange rate at the reporting period end.

questions.q: The foreign currency transaction gain (in UYU millions) on exported goods reported by Celeste in the most recent year is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the answer considers that the foreign transaction gain must be deferred until collection. Therefore, the foreign transaction gain as of 31 December is
UYU 0 million.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the calculation uses as the transaction exchange rate the average rate for the year instead of the exchange rate of 15 November:
Foreign transaction gain = USD 5 million (44.63 – 43.26) = UYU 6.85 million ~
UYU 6.9 million.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because for foreign currency transactions whose settlement dates fall in subsequent accounting periods, both IFRS and US GAAP require adjustments to reflect intervening changes in currency exchange rates. Foreign currency transaction gain and losses are reported on the income statement.
As the export receivable is in USD and the USD appreciated against the UYP from 15 November (42.95 UYU/USD) to 31 December (44.63 UYU/USD), the receivable that remains outstanding as of 31 December generates a foreign transaction gain of:
Foreign transaction gain = USD 5 million (44.63 – 42.95) = UYU 8.4 million

questions.q: Salto’s contribution to Celeste’s consolidated gross profit (in UYU millions) in the most recent year is closest to:
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because Celeste uses the current rate method to translate Salto’s financial statements. Under such methods, revenues and expenses are translated at the exchange rate that existed when the transaction took place. For practical reasons, a rate that approximates the exchange rates at the dates of the transactions, such as an average exchange rate, may be used. Therefore, Salto’s translated gross profit (Salto’s contribution to Celeste’s consolidated gross profit) in the most recent year is:
Gross profit = Revenue (USD) × Average exchange rate – Cost of sales (USD) × Average exchange rate
Gross profit = USD 120 million × 43.26 – USD 65 million × 43.26 = UYU 2,379.3 million ~ UYU 2,379

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it translates revenue and cost of sales using the temporal method, instead of the current rate method.
Gross profit = Revenue (USD) × Average exchange rate – Cost of sales (USD) × Average exchange rate for inventory purchases
Gross profit = USD 120 million × 43.26 – USD 65 million × 42.81 = UYU 2,408.55 million ~ UYU 2,409

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it translates revenue and cost of sales using the end-of-year exchange rate as if those items were balance sheet items.
Gross profit = Revenue (USD) × End-of-year exchange rate – Cost of sales (USD) × End-of-year exchange rate
Gross profit = USD 120 million × 44.63 – USD 65 million × 44.63 = UYU 2,454.65 million ~ UYU 2,455

questions.q: If Monte's results had been translated using the current rate method, its total shareholders' equity would have been:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the method Celeste used to translate Monte’s financial statements (temporal method) resulted in total shareholders’ equity that was lower than it would have been under the current rate method.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the method Celeste used to translate Monte’s financial statements (temporal method) resulted in total shareholders’ equity that was lower than it would have been under the current rate method.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because Celeste uses the temporal method to translate Monte’s financial statements. Under this method, monetary assets and liabilities (in USD) are translated at the current exchange rate, non-monetary assets and liabilities measured at historical cost (in USD) are translated at historical exchange rates.
Monte’s monetary assets and liabilities were translated using the end-of-year exchange rate (44.63 UYU/USD). Monte’s non-monetary assets (the only non-monetary assets are inventory and fixed assets, and all liabilities are monetary) were translated using the average exchange rate prevailing at time of purchase (42.15 UYU/USD). This last exchange rate is lower than the end-of-year exchange rate.
If Celeste had used the method used for Salto to translate Monte’s financial statements (the current rate method), all assets and liabilities (in USD) would have been translated (into UYU) at the current exchange rate at balance sheet date (44.63 UYU/USD).
Therefore, the method Celeste used to translate Monte’s financial statements (temporal method) resulted in total shareholders’ equity that was lower than it would have been under the current rate method.

questions.q: Is Romano correct about the method that Celeste should use to translate the new subsidiary’s financial statements?
options: No, because Celeste should use the temporal method
No, because Celeste should use the average exchange rate for the income statement
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because when a foreign entity is located in a highly inflationary economy IFRS requires that the foreign entity’s financial statements first be restated for local inflation using the procedures outlined in IAS 29. Then, the inflation-restated foreign currency financial statements are translated into the parent’s presentation currency using the current exchange rate.
Therefore, Romano is correct about the method that Celeste should use to translate the new subsidiary’s financial statements.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Celeste should use the method indicated by Romano to translate the new subsidiary’s financial statements, and not the temporal method.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Celeste should use the method indicated by Romano to translate the new subsidiary’s financial statements. This method uses the current exchange rate as of year-end both for the balance sheet and the income statement.

title: Mock 1 · Diamond: factor models, ETF costs, arbitrage
body:
Mary Diamond, a portfolio manager, uses quantitative models for portfolio construction and attribution analysis.
As potential additions to her portfolio, Diamond identifies three ETFs (ETF 1, ETF 2, and ETF 3) that replicate US-based equity indexes. She believes that these ETFs are affected by two common macroeconomic factors: surprises in inflation, FINFL, and surprises in unemployment, FUNEMP. Diamond estimates the following two-factor macroeconomic model equations that describe the returns of each ETF (RETF 1, RETF 2 and RETF 3), where error terms are denoted by εETF 1, εETF 2 and εETF 3,  respectively:
RETF 1 = 0.07 + 1.4FINFL – 0.6FUNEMP + εETF 1
RETF 2 = 0.09 + 0.6FINFL – 0.8FUNEMP + εETF 2
RETF 3 = 0.08 + 1.5FINFL – 0.2FUNEMP + εETF 3
Diamond next estimates the cost of ownership for ETF 1 over a 15-month holding period. She gathers the following information for her estimate:
Round-trip trading commission is 0.05%
Bid-offer spread on purchase and sale is 0.20%
Annual management fee is 0.08%
Diamond uses a fundamental factor model to decompose the active return of an external equity manager's portfolio. Exhibit 1 shows the information used in her analysis. Diamond calculates the manager's active return attributable to security selection to be 1%.
Exhibit 1
Factor	Factor Sensitivity (Manager's portfolio)	Factor Sensitivity (Benchmark)	Factor Return
Factor 1	–1.00	–0.60	–2.00%
Factor 2	0.50	0.25	3.50%
Finally, Diamond identifies three well-diversified portfolios, shown in Exhibit 2. She believes that the expected returns of these portfolios are best modeled with a single-factor model consistent with arbitrage pricing theory.
Exhibit 2
Portfolio	Expected Return	Factor Sensitivity
X	7%	0.50
Y	9%	0.85
Z	11%	1.00
After reviewing the data in Exhibit 2, Diamond concludes that an arbitrage opportunity exists and considers the following three strategies:
Strategy 1: Buy $2,000,000 of Z; sell short $1,600,000 of X and sell short $400,000 of Y
Strategy 2: Buy $600,000 of X and buy $1,400,000 of Z; sell short $2,000,000 of Y
Strategy 3: Buy $200,000 of Y and buy $1,800,000 of Z; sell short $2,000,000 of X

questions.q: Based on the two-factor macroeconomic model, which ETF has the highest expected return?
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because ETF 1 has the lowest expected return of 7%. The intercept term represents the expected return of the asset, which reflects the effects of the predicted values of the macroeconomic variables on expected stock returns. The ETF with the highest expected return will be the one that has the highest intercept term. The expected returns on ETF 1, ETF 2 and ETF 3 are 7%, 9% and 8% respectively. Therefore, ETF 2 has the highest expected return and ETF 1 has the lowest expected return.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because ETF 2 has the highest intercept term of 9%. Macroeconomic factor models analyze the return to an asset in three components, the asset's expected return, its unexpected return resulting from new information about the factors, and an error term. More specifically, the intercept term represents the expected return of the asset, which reflects the effects of the predicted values of the macroeconomic variables on expected stock returns. The ETF with the highest expected return will be the one that has the highest intercept term. The expected returns on ETF 1, ETF 2 and ETF 3 are 7%, 9% and 8% respectively. Therefore, ETF 2 has the highest expected return.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because ETF 3 has the second highest expected return of 8%.ETF 3 has the highest sensitivity to surprises in inflation and the lowest sensitivity to surprises in unemployment. However, these sensitivities are not relevant to expected return. Instead, the intercept term represents the expected return of the asset, which reflects the effects of the predicted values of the macroeconomic variables on expected stock returns. The ETF with the highest expected return will be the one that has the highest intercept term. The expected returns on ETF 1, ETF 2 and ETF 3 are 7%, 9% and 8% respectively. Therefore, ETF 2 has the highest expected return

questions.q: Excluding any compounding effects, the expected total holding period cost of investing in ETF 1 is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this holding period cost assumes that annual management fee is constant and not a function of holding period. 
15-month holding period cost = trading costs (round-trip trading commission and bid-ask spread) and management fees (mistakenly not adjusted for holding period) = 0.05% + 0.20% + 0.08% = 0.33%.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because expected total holding period cost can be estimated as the sum of trading costs (round-trip trading commission and bid-ask spread) and management fees (adjusted for holding period):
15-month holding period cost = 0.05% + 0.20% + (15/12) × 0.08% = 0.35%.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this holding period cost assumes that trading costs are also a function of the holding period. 
15-month holding period cost = [trading costs (round-trip trading commission and bid-ask spread) and management fees] × adjustment for holding period = (0.05% + 0.20% + 0.08%) × (15/12) = 0.4125% ≈ 0.41%.

questions.q: Which of the following had the largest contribution to the manager's active return?
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the tilt on Factor 1 has the smallest contribution (i.e. 0.8% < 1%) to the manager's active return of 2.675%.
Fundamental factor models can be used to decompose active return of a manager into two parts: (1) active return component due to factor tilts and (2) active return component due to security selection. The first component can be calculated as the product of managerial factor tilts and factor returns. Given the information in the exhibit, contribution of factor tilts of each factor can be calculated as:
Contribution of Factor 1 tilt to active return = [(–1.00) – (–0.60)] × (– 2.00%) = 0.8%
Contribution of Factor 2 tilt to active return = (0.50 – 0.25) × 3.50% = 0.875%
Given that security selection is 1%, the active return of the manager's portfolio is 2.675% (= 0.8% + 0.875% + 1 %). Therefore, security selection has the largest contribution to the manager's active return.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because tilt on Factor 2 has the second largest contribution (i.e. 0.875% < 1%) to the manager's active return of 2.675%.

Contribution of Factor 1 tilt to active return = [(–1.00) – (–0.60)] × (– 2.00%) = 0.8%
Contribution of Factor 2 tilt to active return = (0.50 – 0.25) × 3.50% = 0.875%
Given that security selection is 1%, the active return of the manager's portfolio is 2.675% (= 0.8% + 0.875% + 1 %). Therefore, security selection has the largest contribution to the manager's active return.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because security selection of 1% represents the largest contribution to the manager's active return of 2.675%.

Given that security selection is 1%, the active return of the manager's portfolio is 2.675% (= 0.8% + 0.875% + 1 %). Therefore, security selection has the largest contribution to the manager's active return.

questions.q: The arbitrage opportunity identified by Diamond can be best exploited with:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this strategy has a positive factor sensitivity and therefore is not an arbitrage opportunity.
Arbitrage opportunity can be defined as an opportunity to earn an expected positive net profit without risk and with no net investment of money. Therefore, one needs to identify which strategy satisfies this definition and choose the strategy with the highest expected return if multiple strategies provide an arbitrage opportunity.
All three strategies have zero net investment (i.e. long and short side of the trade sum to $2 million), implying that all strategies are valid arbitrage candidates. The next step requires calculating factor sensitivities for each strategy (to ensure that strategies have zero factor sensitivities). These can be calculated as a weighted average of portfolio factor sensitivities (weights are based on dollar amounts):
Strategy 1 Factor sensitivity = 100% × 1.00 – 80% × 0.50 – 20% × 0.85 = 0.430
where 100% = $2m / $2m, –80% = $1.6m / $2m and –20% = $0.4m / $2m
Strategy 2 Factor sensitivity = 30% × 0.50 + 70% × 1.00 – 100% × 0.85 = 0
where 30% = $0.6m / $2m, 70% = $1.4m / $2m and 100% = $2m / $2m
Strategy 3 Factor sensitivity = 10% × 0.85 + 90% × 1.00 – 100% × 0.50 = 0.485
where 10% = $0.2m / $2m, 90% = $1.8m / $2m and 100% = $2m / $2m
Only Strategy 2 has zero factor sensitivity and therefore Strategy 2 can be the only arbitrage opportunity. The other two strategies have positive factor sensitivities, thus any return they offer will be due to risk exposure but not due to arbitrage.

These can be calculated as a weighted average of portfolio factor sensitivities (weights are based on dollar amounts):
Strategy 1 Factor sensitivity = 100% × 1.00 – 80% × 0.50 – 20% × 0.85 = 0.430
where 100% = $2m / $2m, –80% = $1.6m / $2m and –20% = $0.4m / $2m
Strategy 2 Factor sensitivity = 30% × 0.50 + 70% × 1.00 – 100% × 0.85 = 0
where 30% = $0.6 m / $2m, 70% = $1.4 m / $2m and 100% = $2m / $2m
Strategy 3 Factor sensitivity = 10% × 0.85 + 90% × 1.00 – 100% × 0.50 = 0.485
where 10% = $0.2 m / $2m, 90% = $1.8m / $2m and 100% = $2m / $2m
Only Strategy 2 has zero factor sensitivity and therefore Strategy 2 can be the only arbitrage opportunity. The other two strategies have positive factor sensitivities thus any return they offer will be due to risk exposure but not due to arbitrage.

title: Mock 1 · Podlasky: growth models
body:
Andrew Podlasky is an analyst at an investment management firm. He is reviewing growth prospects under different economic models for Country A and Country B.
First, Podlasky reviews the macroeconomic data of Country A and Country B in Exhibit 1 to determine the current steady-state growth rates and potential GDP growth rates of both countries.
Exhibit 1
 	Country A	Country B
Growth rate in the labor force	0.9%	0.5%
Labor cost in total factor cost	55.2%	56.4%
Growth rate in labor productivity	3.5%	2.3%
Growth rate of total factor productivity	2.1%	1.5%
 
Country A, which is currently operating at steady-state of growth, has announced its intentions to remove trade barriers on capital investments. As a result, Podlasky concludes that the country's economic growth rate per capita will increase permanently.
For Country B, Podlasky estimates that the output gap, defined as the difference between the real growth rate in potential GDP and short-term real GDP growth, has widened by 0.8 percentage points as a result of the following revisions:
A 0.2% higher estimated real growth rate in potential GDP
A 0.6% lower estimate of real growth in short-term GDP

questions.q: Based on the neoclassical model, the steady-state growth rate for Country A is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it omits growth in the labor force from the steady-state growth rate calculation: 
ΔY/Y = θ/(1 – α) + n = 2.1%/(0.552) + 0.9% = 3.8044 ≈ 3.8%

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because in order to calculate the steady-state growth rate under the neoclassical model, growth rate of total factor productivity is scaled by labor factor share and added to growth rate in the labor force
ΔY/Y = θ/(1 – α) + n = 2.1%/(0.552) + 0.9% = 4.7044 ≈ 4.7%
where:
ΔY/Y = steady state growth rate
θ = growth rate of total factor productivity = 2.1%
α = elasticity of output with respect to capital
1 – α = labor cost in total factor cost = labor share of output = 0.552
n = growth rate in the labor force = 0.9%

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it misinterprets the elasticity of output due to labor productivity:
α = elasticity of output with respect to labor (instead of capital)
1 – α =1 – elasticity of output with respect to labor = 1 – 0.552 = 0.448
ΔY/Y = θ/(1 – α) + n = 2.1%/(0.448) + 0.9% = 0.0559 ≈ 5.6%

questions.q: Based on the labor productivity growth accounting equation, the potential GDP growth rate of Country B is:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it adds total factor productivity growth instead of the growth rate in labor productivity.
Growth rate in potential GDP = Growth rate in the labor force + Growth rate in labor productivity  + Growth rate of total factor productivity = 0.5% + 2.3% + 1.5% = 2.0%

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because as per labor productivity growth accounting equation, growth rate in potential GDP is calculated as the sum of the growth rate in labor force and growth rate in labor productivity. 
Growth rate in potential GDP = Growth rate in the labor force + Growth rate in labor productivity = 0.5% + 2.3% = 2.8% 

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it adds growth rate of total factor productivity to the equation.
Growth rate in potential GDP = Growth rate in the labor force + Growth rate in labor productivity + growth rate of total factor productivity = 0.5% + 2.3% + 1.5% = 4.3%

questions.q: Which of the following models would best support Podlasky's conclusion regarding the impact of removing Country A's trade barriers?
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because under the classical growth model no factor can lead to economic growth level rising permanently. Per capita economic growth under the classical model is only temporary because an exploding population with limited resources brings growth to an end.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because although under the neoclassical model: opening up the economy to trade and financial flows can significantly affect the rate of growth in an economy; however, this does not permanently raise the rate of economic growth. In the Solow model, after the reallocation of world savings, there is no permanent increase in the rate of growth in an economy. In contrast to the neoclassical model, endogenous growth models predict that a more open trade policy will permanently raise the rate of economic growth.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because open trade (removing trade barriers) fosters innovation and through selection, scale and backwardness effects, international trade will increase output. In contrast to the neoclassical model, endogenous growth models predict that a more open trade policy will permanently raise the rate of economic growth. Faster capital accumulation translates one for one into faster growth in output per capita.

questions.q: Podlasky's revisions to the growth forecasts for Country B most likely imply:
options: lower expected long-term equity returns and higher expected short-term inflation.
higher expected long-term equity returns and lower expected short-term inflation.
higher expected long-term equity returns and higher expected short-term inflation.
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the output gap is widening. A higher growth rate in potential GDP implies higher — not lower — long-term equity returns. Also, short-term GDP growth below(above) the potential GDP growth rate puts downward(upward) pressure on inflation, which puts corresponding pressure on nominal interest rates and bond prices.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because a higher estimated growth rate in potential GDP implies higher long-term equity returns. Also, a lower estimate of short-term GDP implies lower expected short-term inflation.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the output gap is widening. A higher estimated growth rate in potential GDP implies a higher and not lower long-term equity returns. Also, a lower estimate of short-term GDP growth implies lower and not higher expected short-term inflation.

title: Mock 1 · Wu: options and delta hedging
body:
Julie Wu is a US-based hedge fund manager. To value the options in her fund, Wu uses both the Black–Scholes–Merton (BSM) and binomial option pricing models.
Wu sells 10 call option contracts on a non-dividend-paying stock, Skyview Corporation, at the value determined by the BSM model, and considers delta-hedging the position using Skyview shares. Each call option contract is for 100 shares. Wu collects the information in Exhibit 1 for a call option on Skyview.
Exhibit 1
Current share price of Skyview	$50
Exercise price of Skyview call option	$50
d1	0.111
d2	–0.049
N(d1)	0.544
N(d2)	0.480
Gamma	0.050
Theta (daily)	–0.018
BSM call value	$3.305
Wu next considers an American-style put option on Wilbo Corporation that matures in two years. She values it with a two-period binomial option pricing model and collects the relevant information in Exhibit 2. Wilbo does not pay dividends.

Exhibit 2
Current share price of Wilbo	$100
Exercise price of Wilbo put option	$98
Risk-free rate (compounded annually)	5%
Risk-neutral probability	0.625
Up factor (u)	1.20
Down factor (d)	0.80
Stock prices in one year	S+ = $120,
S- = $80
Stock prices in two years	S++ = $144,
S+- = $96,
S-- = $64

questions.q: To delta hedge her call option position on Skyview, how many shares of Skyview should Wu buy?
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this number of shares is based on (1 – N(d1)) = 1 – 0.544 = 0.456.  Since each call option contract is for 100 shares and Wu sells 10 contracts, we get 0.456 × 100 × 10 = 456 shares.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the number of shares is calculated based on N(d2) = 0.480 rather than N(d1) = 0.544. Since each call option contract is for 100 shares and Wu sells 10 contracts, we get 0.480 × 100 × 10 = 480 shares.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because, based on the BSM model, the correct number of shares to buy per option sold is equal to N(d1) = 0.544 since Skyview is a non-dividend-paying stock. Since each call option contract sold is for 100 shares and Wu sells 10 contracts, the correct number of shares to purchase for the delta hedge is 0.544 × 100 × 10 = 544 shares.

questions.q: The gamma of Wu's delta-hedged position would be:
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because, for Wu's delta-hedged position, we are long the stock (which has zero gamma) and short the call (short call gamma is negative). The call has positive gamma and since we are short, the call position in our portfolio will have negative gamma, leaving us with an overall gamma that is negative (short call/long stock combined).

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the delta-hedged position that includes a short call will have negative gamma even though the long stock position has zero gamma. 

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the delta-hedged position with a short call will have negative gamma. The call itself has positive gamma and since we are short, the call position in our portfolio will have negative gamma.

questions.q: Holding all else constant, the value of the call on Skyview one day after Wu's sale will be closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it incorrectly uses gamma = 0.05 in place of theta: Option value 1 day later = current option value minus gamma = $3.305 – $0.050 = $3.255.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the calculation of how option value changes given the passage of time (1 day, assuming all else constant) is given by daily theta = –0.018. The initial option value is $3.305 and, after 1 day, the option value would be $3.305 – $0.018 = $3.287.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it adds the effect of theta rather than subtracting it: $3.305 + $0.018 = $3.323.

questions.q: Using the two-period binomial option pricing model, the value of the American put on Wilbo Corporation is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this is the European put price. 
Calculations based on this are as follows (risk-neutral probability = 0.625, which is given):
Ending stock prices at T = 2 (given in Exhibit 2) and put prices (X = 98) are:
u×u×S = 144 and Puu = 0
u×d×S = 96 and Pud = 2
d×d×S = 64 and Pdd = 34
Put prices at T = 1 are the PV of the expected T = 2 put prices as follows:
Stock price = u×S = 120; Put value = [0.625(0) + 0.375(2)]/1.05 = 0.7143
Stock price = d×S = 80; Put value = [0.625(2) + 0.375(34)]/1.05 = 13.3333
Working backwards to T = 0, we have the European put value as the PV of the expected T = 1 values as follows:
Put value = [0.625(0.7143) + 0.375(13.3333)]/1.05 = 5.19

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the put is correctly exercised when the stock price at T = 1 is equal to 80. Calculations based on this are as follows (risk-neutral probability = 0.625, which is given):
Ending stock prices at T = 2 and put prices (X = 98) are:
u×u×S = 144 and Puu = 0
u×d×S = 96 and Pud = 2
d×d×S = 64 and Pdd = 34
Put prices at T = 1 are the PV of the expected T = 2 put prices as follows
(will first show European values): 
Stock price = u×S = 120;  Put value = [0.625(0) + 0.375(2)]/1.05 = 0.7143
Stock price = d×S = 80;    Put value = [0.625(2) + 0.375(34)]/1.05 = 13.3333
At T = 1, when the stock price is d×S = 80, the exercised value (X = 98) is 18, therefore it is optimal to exercise because 18 > 13.3333.
Working backwards to T = 0, we have the American put value as the PV of the expected T = 1 values as follows:
Put value = [0.625(0.7143) + 0.375(18)]/1.05 = 6.85

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because, in the calculation of the expected payoff, the option values associated with the "up" stock prices are multiplied by 1 – p rather than p (and p for the associated down values). Calculations are as follows and p = 0.625. 
Ending stock prices at T = 2 and put prices (X = 98) are:
u×u×S = 144 and Puu = 0
u×d×S = 96 and Pud = 2
d×d×S = 64 and Pdd = 34
Put prices at T = 1 are the PV of the expected T = 2 put prices as follows
(will first show European values): 
Stock price = u×S = 120;  Put value = [0.375(0) + 0.625(2)]/1.05 = 1.1905
Stock price = d×S = 80;    Put value = [0.375(2) + 0.625(34)]/1.05 = 20.9524 (i.e., do not exercise since exercised value is 18)
Working backwards to T = 0, we have the American put value as the PV of the expected T = 1 values as follows:
Put value = [0.375(1.1905) + 0.625(20.9524)]/1.05 = 12.90.

title: Mock 1 · Alison: Apex earnings quality and acquisition
body:
Zachary Alison is analyzing the earnings and financial reporting quality of Apex, a consumer electronics manufacturer. The company reports its financial statements according to US GAAP.
In Exhibit 1, Alison compiles selected financial statement data for Apex for the year just ended. Alison then assesses the company's earnings quality by calculating the cash-flow-based accruals ratio. 
Exhibit 1
 	Year Just Ended
($ millions)	Prior Year
($ millions)
Net operating assets	280	229
Net income	83	64
Operating cash flow	113	77
Investing cash flow	(58)	(39)
Financing cash flow	5	0
When reviewing the notes to Apex's most recent financial statements, Alison observes that some inventory is held in preparation for product launches. This inventory is not expected to be sold within one year and was reclassified as other non-current assets in the year just ended. This is the first year Apex has made such a reclassification. Alison determines how the reclassification affects its financial ratios. 
Apex recently announced that it will purchase an 80% interest in Beast Electronics (Beast) for $24 million and will gain control over Beast. Beast's identifiable net assets have a fair value of $25 million and the fair value of the entire company is $30 million.

questions.q: Apex's cash-flow-based accruals ratio for the year just ended is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because financing cash flow is included in the calculation as follows:
= [NI1 − (CFO1 + CFI1+ CFF1] / [(NOA1 + NOA0) / 2]
= [83 − [113 + (–58) + 5]] / [(280 + 229) / 2]
= [83 − (60)] / [(509) / 2]
= 23 / 254.5 ≈ 9%

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because net operating assets of the year just ended is used instead of average net operating assets as follows:
= [NI1 − (CFO1 + CFI1)] / NOA1
= [83 − [113 + (–58)]] / 280
= [83 − (55)] / 280
= 28 / 280 = 10%

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the cash flow accruals ratio for the year just ended is 11% as follows:
= [NI1 − (CFO1 + CFI1)] / [(NOA1 + NOA0) / 2]
where:
NI = net income
CFO = cash flow from operations
CFI = cash flow from investing
NOA = net operating assets
= [83 − [113 + (–58)]] / [(280 + 229) / 2]
= [83 − (55)] / [(509) / 2]
= 28 / 254.5 ≈ 11%

questions.q: As a result of Apex's reclassification of its inventory in the year that has just ended, which of the following ratios most likely increased?
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Apex's reclassifies its inventory, which is part of current assets, to other non-current assets therefore the current ratio will decrease because current assets will decrease and current liabilities will stay the same.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the inventory turnover calculated using the reported inventory number will most likely increase because the amount of inventory relative to cost of goods sold will decrease.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the number of days of inventory on hand calculated using the reported inventory number will most likely decrease because the amount of inventory relative to cost of goods sold will decrease.

questions.q: Apex should account for its purchase of Beast using the:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because if Apex is deemed to have control over Beast, it would use the acquisition method to account for Beast in its consolidated financial statements. The equity method is used for some joint ventures and when there is significant influence but not control. In this case, Apex has an 80% stake and has control over Beast.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because if Apex is deemed to have control over Beast, it would use the acquisition method to account for Beast in its consolidated financial statements. In this case, Apex has an 80% stake and has control over Beast.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because if Apex is deemed to have control over Beast, it would use the acquisition method to account for Beast in its consolidated financial statements. Proportionate consolidation is used for joint ventures. In this case, Apex has an 80% stake and has control over Beast.

questions.q: As a result of its purchase of Beast, Apex should recognize goodwill of:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Apex reports under US GAAP, and should report $5 million under the full goodwill method. This would be the amount reported under the partial goodwill method. Partial goodwill = Fair value of consideration – Share of fair value of identifiable net assets = $24 million – 80% × $ 25 million = $24 million – $20 million = $4 million.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because Apex reports under US GAAP, and should report $5 million under the full goodwill method. Full goodwill = Fair value of entity – Fair value of identifiable net assets = $30 million – $25 million = $5 million.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Apex reports under US GAAP, and should report $5 million under the full goodwill method. If acquisition cost was used instead of fair value of identifiable net assets then full goodwill would = $30 million – $24 million = $6 million.

title: Mock 1 · Zern: LuftComm residual income
body:
Nicole Zern, an equity analyst, is reviewing preliminary research reports developed by her team for two wireless telecommunications companies: LuftComm and PrimaNet. 
LuftComm
After reviewing the preliminary report for LuftComm, Zern decides to revise it slightly. She notes that interest expense is tax-deductible and collects the selected financial data for LuftComm shown in Exhibit 1. 
Exhibit 1
Book value of total assets at beginning of the year (millions)	€5,000

ROE	22.1%

Pretax cost of debt	6.0%
Market price per share	€44.65
P/B ratio	1.90
Assuming the clean surplus relation holds, Zern uses the data in Exhibit 1 to calculate residual income for the year and then estimates the implied growth rate of earnings for LuftComm based on the current market price.
PrimaNet
Zern first notes that the team's preliminary report on PrimaNet uses a multistage residual income model with a persistence factor of 0.12, one-quarter of the industry average of 0.48.
Zern next assumes the clean surplus relation holds, and uses the data in Exhibit 2 to update the report based on a finite-horizon multistage residual income model.
Exhibit 2

questions.q: The residual income for LuftComm is closest to:
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because LuftComm’s residual income of €122 million can be calculated using net income and the equity charge (Residual Income = Net Income – Equity Charge) or using net operating profit after taxes and the total capital charge (NOPAT = EBIT × (1 – Tax rate)).

Option 1:
Using Net Income and the Equity Charge (values in € millions):
EBIT	700
Less: Interest Expense	(180)
= Pretax Income	520
Less: Income Taxes 	(78)
= Net Income  	 442

Equity Charge = Book Value of Equity × Cost of Equity
Equity Charge = (Book Value of Assets – Book Value of Debt) × Cost of Equity
Equity Charge = (5,000 – 3,000) × 0.16 = 320
 
Residual Income = Net Income – Equity Charge
Residual Income = 442 – 320 = 122
 
Option 2:
Using NOPAT and the Total Capital Charge (Values in € millions):

NOPAT = EBIT × (1 – Tax Rate) 
NOPAT= 700 × (1 – 0.15) = 595

Debt Charge = Book Value of Debt × Pretax Cost of Debt × (1 – Tax Rate)
Debt Charge = 3,000 × 0.06 × (1 – 0.15) = 153

Total Capital Charge = Debt Charge + Equity Charge
Total Capital Charge = 153 + 320 = 473
 
Residual Income = NOPAT – Total Capital Charge
Residual Income = 595 – 473 = 122

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because €200 million is mistakenly derived by using pretax earnings instead of net income in the residual income calculation (values in € millions):
EBIT	700
Less: Interest Expense	(180)
= Pretax Income	520
Less: Income Taxes 	<OMITTED>
= Net Income  	 520

Equity Charge = Book Value of Equity × Cost of Equity
Equity Charge = (Book Value of Assets – Book Value of Debt) × Cost of Equity
Equity Charge = (5,000 – 3,000) × 0.16 = 320

Incorrect Residual Income = Incorrect Net Income – Equity Charge
Incorrect Residual Income = 520 – 320 = 200

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because €275 million is mistakenly derived due to the deduction of the equity charge from NOPAT instead of Net Income. That is, it fails to consider the debt charge when using the NOPAT approach to computing Residual Income (values in € millions):

NOPAT = EBIT × (1 – Tax Rate)
