questions.q: Based on the single-stage residual income model, the implied growth rate of earnings for LuftComm is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because 6.1% is the difference between ROE and the cost of equity. Incorrect implied growth rate = 22.1% – 16.0% = 6.1%

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the implied growth rate of earnings from the single-stage residual income model is calculated by solving for g in the following equation:
V0 = B0 + B0[(ROE – r)/ (r – g)]
which gives the following:
g = r – [((ROE – r) × B0)/ (V0 – B0)].
Book value per share can be calculated using the given price-to-book ratio and market price per share as follows:
Book value per share (B0) = Market price per share/Price-to-book ratio
Book value per share (B0) = 44.65 / 1.90 = 23.50
Using the market price per share (44.65) as V0, the book value (23.50) as B0, the ROE (22.1%), and the cost of equity (16%) as r, the implied growth rate (g) can be solved as follows:
g = r – [((ROE – r) × B0) / (V0 – B0)]
g = 0.160 – [((0.221 – 0.160) × 23.50) / (44.65 – 23.50)] = 0.09222 ≈ 9.2% 

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because of the omission of the initial book value of equity (B0) as the first term in the single-stage residual income model.
Correct Formula:  V0 = B0 + B0[(ROE – r)/ (r – g)]
Incorrect Formula:  V0 = [(ROE – r) / (r – g)] B0
Incorrect g = r – [((ROE – r) × B0)/ V0]
Incorrect g = 0.160 – [((0.221 – 0.160) × 23.50) / 44.65] = 0.1279 ≈ 12.8%

questions.q: Relative to the industry, the persistence factor used in the preliminary report on PrimaNet is most consistent with the firm having:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because PrimaNet’s persistence is lower than the industry average, which is inconsistent with low dividend payouts. Instead, low dividend payout is associated with higher residual income persistence.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because PrimaNet’s persistence is lower than the industry average, which is inconsistent with low levels of accounting rates of return (ROE). Instead, high or extreme levels of accounting return (ROE) are associated with lower residual income persistence. 

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the persistence factor utilized in the preliminary report on PrimaNet is significantly lower than the industry average. High or extreme levels of accounting accruals is consistent with lower residual income persistence.

questions.q: Based on the finite-horizon multistage residual income model, PrimaNet's intrinsic value per share is closest to:
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the intrinsic value per share of €24.91 is calculated by adding the present value of residual income in Year 1, present value of income in Year 2, and the present value of the terminal value (premium of market value over book value) at the end of Year 2.

Where:
V0 = Intrinsic value per share today
B0 = Book value per share today = €18.50 in Exhibit 2
The middle term is the sum of the present values of residual income for each year of the forecast period = €2.25 for Year 1 and €2.00 for Year 2
PT = market price at the end of the forecast period = €26.50
BT = book value at the end of the forecast period = €23.75
r = cost of equity = 12.8%
V0 = 18.50 + 2.25 + 2.00 + [(26.50 - 23.75) / (1.128)2] = €24.91

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it mistakenly uses the WACC (6.5%) as the discount rate for the premium over book value at the end of Year 2 (Terminal Value of 2.75) instead of the cost of equity (12.80%).
Incorrect V0 = 18.50 + 2.25 + 2.00 + [(26.50 - 23.75) / (1.065)2] = €25.17

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it fails to discount the present value of premium (market price less book value) at the end of Year 2 (terminal value of 2.75).
Incorrect V0 = 18.50 + 2.25 + 2.00 + (26.50 - 23.75) = €25.50

title: Mock 1 · Souza: Franca active management
body:
Carl Souza is a portfolio manager with Franca Advisors.
During a client meeting, Souza presents current economic data and Franca's forecasts for next year, as shown in Exhibit 1. The client asks Souza to identify a sector that should experience the smallest decrease in profitability under Franca's forecast.
Exhibit 1
Economic Indicator	Current	Forecast
Nominal GDP growth rate	5.00%	4.50%
Inflation rate	3.00%	5.00%
Unemployment rate	3.75%	5.25%
Souza tells prospective clients that based on his bottom-up security selection, he has delivered strong risk-adjusted returns relative to his benchmark. To illustrate his portfolio's performance, he provides data for the past five years shown in Exhibit 2. The average risk-free rate was 3.50% over this period.
Exhibit 2
 	Portfolio	Benchmark
Average annual return	7.50%	5.60%
Standard deviation of returns	15.00%	12.00%
Active risk	5.00%	---
Souza uses the fundamental law of active management in portfolio construction. He is analyzing the information coefficient and target active risk to determine what actions would result in smaller optimal active weights for his portfolio.
A prospective client has equity portfolio guidelines that restrict the maximum overweights and underweights on industry sectors. Souza evaluates the effect of these guidelines.

questions.q: Based on Franca's forecasts, which of the following sectors will most likely have the smallest decrease in profitability next year?
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the data in Exhibit 1 forecasts a contraction in the economy (negative real GDP growth) over the next year. Companies that produce durable goods would see earnings fall substantially in this type of economic environment. We can expect then that the profits of companies that produce durable as opposed to non-durable goods to be commensurately more volatile too.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the data in Exhibit 1 forecasts a contraction in the economy over the next year. Nominal GDP growth will decline from 5.00% to 4.50% and real GDP growth from 2.00% to –0.50%, and the unemployment rate will increase by 1.50 percentage points. Recessions are associated with declines in employment, incomes, output, and, subsequently, profitability. Cyclical sectors are represented by companies that produce discretionary consumer goods, whereas the non-cyclical index is represented by an index that includes companies that produce staple (or less discretionary) consumer goods. The demand for staples will remain fairly stable over the business cycle.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the data in Exhibit 1 forecasts a contraction in the economy (negative real GDP growth) over the next year. Companies that produce discretionary consumer goods would see earnings fall substantially in this type of economic environment.

questions.q: The information ratio for Souza's portfolio over the past five years is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because in this calculation, the Sharpe ratio, (RP – RF)/σP, was calculated instead of the information ratio, (7.50% – 3.50%)/15.00% = 4.00%/15.00% = 0.27.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the information ratio (IR) is calculated as:
IR = (RP – RB)/σ(RP – RB) = RA/σA = (7.50% – 5.60%)/5.00% = 1.90%/5.00% = 0.38.
IR compares a portfolio's active return relative to a benchmark with the volatility of the active return or active risk.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because in this calculation, the risk-free rate was used rather than the benchmark return, (7.50% – 3.50%)/5.00% = 4.00%/5.00% = 0.80.

questions.q: Which of the following would most likely result in Souza's desired change of optimal active weights?
options: A decrease in both the information coefficient and the target active risk
An increase in the information coefficient and a decrease in the target active risk
A decrease in the information coefficient and an increase in the target active risk
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because investors with higher IC, or ability to forecast returns, will add more value over time but only to the extent that those forecasts are exploited in the construction of the managed portfolio. So, a higher information coefficient results in smaller optimal active weights.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because investors with higher IC, or ability to forecast returns, will add more value over time but only to the extent that those forecasts are exploited in the construction of the managed portfolio. So, a higher information coefficient results in smaller optimal active weights. In addition, the desire for more active portfolio risk requires larger individual active weights. So, a lower target active risk results in smaller optimal active weights.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because investors with higher IC, or ability to forecast returns, will add more value over time but only to the extent that those forecasts are exploited in the construction of the managed portfolio. So, a higher information coefficient results in smaller optimal active weights. In addition, the desire for more active portfolio risk requires larger individual active weights. So, a lower target active risk results in smaller active weights.

questions.q: The most likely effect of the prospective client's equity portfolio guidelines is a reduction in:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because breadth refers to the number of independent decisions. The guidelines restrict the weightings but not the number of decisions.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the prospective client has imposed constraints on portfolio construction. The long-only and maximum over- or underweight constraints substantially reduce the transfer of active return forecasts into active weights.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the information coefficient is independent of client guidelines or constraints but rather relates to the investor's capability in forecasting. IC is the ex ante information coefficient that measures the assumed accuracy of the investor’s relative rankings.

title: Mock 1 · Eng: Treasury term structure and key rate duration
body:
Michael Eng manages institutional client portfolios of US Treasury securities. He expects that spot rates one year from now will be the same as they are today. Eng implements a strategy of rolling down the yield curve in one of the managed portfolios. Current information on rates is shown in Exhibit 1.
Exhibit 1
Spot Rate	1-year Implied Forward Rate
r(1) = 0.75%	f(0,1) = 0.75%
r(2) = 1.20%	f(1,1) = 1.65%
r(3) = 1.45%	f(2,1) = 1.95%
r(4) = 1.65%	f(3,1) = 2.25%
Eng is reviewing the portfolios of his two largest clients. Client 1 restricts Eng to buy only bonds with maturities of three years or less. Even though Eng expects the return of 5-year maturity bonds to be superior to that of 3-year maturity bonds, he continues to invest in 3-year maturities for Client 1's portfolio.
Client 2's portfolio consists of 1-year, 3-year and 5-year zero-coupon bonds and has an effective duration of 3.20. Eng is concerned about the effect a twist in the yield curve would have on this portfolio. The portfolio's 1-year key rate duration is 0.25 and its 3-year key rate duration is 1.10.

questions.q: The current yield to maturity (YTM) on a default-free, 1.2% annual-pay, three-year coupon bond is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this is the coupon on the bond, not the YTM. It would be the correct answer if the bond was priced at par. Given the term structure in the exhibit, the bond is not priced at par.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the YTM on a three-year coupon bond will be closest to the three-year spot rate, regardless of coupon. The three-year spot rate is 1.45%. 
The price of the bond is calculated as the present value of cash flows. 
PV = PMT/(1 + z1)1 + PMT/(1 +z2)2 + PMT + 100/(1 + z3)3,
Where PMT = coupon and z = spot rate for each time period.
PV = 1.2/1.0075+1.2/1.0122+101.2/1.01453 = 1.19107 + 1.17171 + 96.9224 = 99.2852. 
Next, solve for YTM: PV = –99.2852, FV=100, n=3, PMT=1.2 and solving for I/Y = YTM = 1.445% ≈ 1.45%.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this is the one-year forward rate in three years, not the YTM for a three-year bond.

questions.q: Given Eng's expectation for spot rates, the first-year return on a 3-year zero-coupon bond is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this is the 1-year spot rate. This rate would only have been achieved if the spot rates evolved as implied by the current forward curve. This is not the case under Eng's expectation of an unchanged spot curve.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this is the 3-year spot rate. Eng would realize the one-year forward rate for year 3, not the geometric average of the forward rates over the three years.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because under Eng's spot curve expectation the total return will be the one-year forward rate for year 3. We can see that if the spot rate curve is unchanged, then each bond rolls down the curve and earns the forward rate.
This can be shown mathematically by calculating the price of a 3-year zero coupon bond today. Price = 1/(1 + spot rate)3 = 1/(1.01453) = 0.957732. With an unchanged yield curve, this bond will become a 2-year zero coupon bond in one year with a price = 1/(1 + spot rate)2 = 1/(1.01202) = 0.976425. The first year return = 0.976425/0.957732 – 1 ≈ 1.95%, which equals f(2,1) from Exhibit 1.

questions.q: Client 1's restriction regarding the securities Eng can purchase is most consistent with the assumptions underlying the:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the preferred habitat theory postulates that if the expected additional returns to be gained become large enough, institutions will be willing to deviate from their preferred maturities or habitats. Eng is not able to do that due to his investor-imposed constraints.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the liquidity preference theory focuses on investor's risk aversion and the fact that they demand a liquidity premium for added interest rate risk. Eng would prefer to invest in longer-term maturities to capture this premium but cannot. Also, Client 1 does not direct Eng to purchase only three-year maturity bonds to capture a possible liquidity premium, but that Eng can purchase securities up to three years. This direction indicates the client does not have a preference to capture the liquidity premium if it exists. Liquidity preference theory asserts that liquidity premiums exist to compensate investors for the added interest rate risk they face when lending long term and that these premiums increase with maturity.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because due to the direction from the Client, Eng continues to invest only in 3-year maturities even though he expects 5-year maturities to offer superior expected returns. The segmented markets theory assumes that market participants are either unwilling or unable to invest in anything other than securities of their preferred maturity. It follows that the yield of securities of a particular maturity is determined entirely by the supply and demand for funds of that particular maturity.

questions.q: The 5-year key rate duration for Client 2's portfolio is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this is the value that would be obtained if 5-year key rate duration is calculated as the 3-year key rate duration plus the 1-year key rate duration plus the 1-year key rate duration to get five full years of key rate duration. This incorrect calculation is: 1.10 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 1.60. 

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because for Portfolio 2 the sum of the three portfolio key rate durations must equal the portfolio's effective duration. Effective duration = 1-year key rate duration + 3-year key rate duration + 5-year key rate duration = 3.20 = 0.25 + 1.10 + 5-year key rate duration. 5-year key rate duration = 3.20 – 0.25 – 1.10 = 1.85.
Key rate duration measures the portfolio risk exposure to each key rate. If all the key rates move by the same amount, then the yield curve has made a parallel shift, and as a result, the proportional change in value has to be consistent with effective duration.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this is the value that would be obtained if the key rate duration curve is assumed to be linear calculated as the 3-year key rate duration plus the 3-year key rate duration less the 1-year key rate duration = 1.10 + (1.10 – 0.25) = 1.95.

title: Mock 1 · Silva: cointegration and feature selection
body:
Alice Silva is a quantitative analyst focusing on the real estate sector.
Silva studies the extent to which private construction spending is affected by public construction spending. She collects data (in $ millions) on total private (PRIV) and public (PUBL) construction spending for the last 363 months and log-transforms both time series.
To determine whether the two log-transformed time series are cointegrated, Silva tests the following null hypotheses:
Null Hypothesis 1: ln(PRIVt) has a unit root.
Null Hypothesis 2: ln(PUBLt) has a unit root.
Null Hypothesis 3: The error term of the linear regression between ln(PRIVt) and ln(PUBLt) has a unit root.
Silva forecasts future private construction spending. She estimates an autoregressive model of order 1 (AR(1)), where Δln(PRIVt) = ln(PRIVt) – ln(PRIVt–1). Silva uses the estimates of the AR(1) model in Exhibit 1 to determine the mean-reverting level of Δln(PRIVt).
Exhibit 1
 	Coefficient	Standard Error	t-Statistic
Intercept	0.00259	0.00073	3.52
ln(PRIVt–1) – ln(PRIVt–2)	0.38616	0.39980	0.97
Next, Silva estimates an AR(1) model for public construction spending, where Δln(PUBLt) = ln(PUBLt) – ln(PUBLt–1). She calculates the residuals (ε) and squared residuals (ε2) of the AR(1) model and estimates the following two linear regressions:
Residual Regression 1: εt = a0 + a1 εt–1 + ut
Residual Regression 2: εt2 = a0 + a1 εt–12 + ut
The t-statistic for the slope coefficients (a1) is 0.70 for Residual Regression 1 and 2.94 for Residual Regression 2. The relevant critical value for these tests is 1.97.
Finally, Silva develops a sentiment indicator for the real estate market. She obtains text data from real estate listings and classifies each listing as "hot," "medium," or "cold" based on how quickly the property sold. After preparing and wrangling the unstructured data, she performs feature selection. She wants to remove noise features and only select the tokens that tend to occur more often in a particular class of text.

questions.q: The time series ln(PRIVt) and ln(PUBLt) are cointegrated if the tests performed by Silva:
options: fail to reject all three null hypotheses.
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because, to be cointegrated, two time series need to satisfy the following criteria:
They both have a unit root, i.e., Null Hypothesis 1 and 2 are not rejected (by a Dickey–Fuller test).
The residuals of the regression between the two time series do not have a unit root, i.e., Null Hypothesis 3 is rejected (by an Engle–Granger Dickey–Fuller test).
When testing for cointegration, five scenarios are possible, and only one of them (Scenario 4) corresponds to cointegration:
Scenario 1: Neither time series has a unit root.
Scenario 2: Only the first time series has a unit root.
Scenario 3: Only the second time series has a unit root.
Scenario 4 (cointegration): Both time series have a unit root and the error term of a linear regression between the two time series does not have a unit root.
Scenario 5: Both time series have a unit root and the error term of a linear regression between the two time series also has a unit root.
If Silva fails to reject Null Hypothesis 1 and 2 and rejects Null Hypothesis 3, we are in Scenario 4 (cointegration): Both time series have a unit root (Null Hypothesis 1 and 2) and the error term of the regression does not have a unit root (Null Hypothesis 3).
If the (Engle–Granger) Dickey–Fuller test rejects the null hypothesis that the error term has a unit root, then we may assume that the error term in the regression is covariance stationary and that the two time series are cointegrated.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because, if Null Hypothesis 1 and 2 are rejected, neither time series has a unit root, which means they cannot be cointegrated.
When testing for cointegration, five scenarios are possible, and only one of them (Scenario 4) corresponds to cointegration:
Scenario 1: Neither time series has a unit root.
Scenario 2: Only the first time series has a unit root.
Scenario 3: Only the second time series has a unit root.
Scenario 4 (cointegration): Both time series have a unit root and the error term of a linear regression between the two time series does not have a unit root.
Scenario 5: Both time series have a unit root and the error term of a linear regression between the two time series also has a unit root.
If Silva rejects Null Hypothesis 1 and 2, we are in Scenario 1, which does not correspond to cointegration. 

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because, if Null Hypothesis 3 is not rejected (by an Engle–Granger Dickey–Fuller test), the residuals of the regression have a unit root and the two time series are not cointegrated. If the (Engle–Granger) Dickey–Fuller test fails to reject the null hypothesis that the error term has a unit root, then we conclude that the error term in the regression is not covariance stationary. Therefore, the two time series are not cointegrated.
When testing for cointegration, five scenarios are possible, and only one of them (Scenario 4) corresponds to cointegration:
Scenario 1: Neither time series has a unit root.
Scenario 2: Only the first time series has a unit root.
Scenario 3: Only the second time series has a unit root.
Scenario 4 (cointegration): Both time series have a unit root and the error term of a linear regression between the two time series does not have a unit root.
Scenario 5: Both time series have a unit root and the error term of a linear regression between the two time series also has a unit root.
If Silva fails to reject all three null hypotheses, we are in Scenario 5, which does not correspond to cointegration: Both time series have a unit root (Null Hypothesis 1 and 2) and the error term of the regression also has a unit root (Null Hypothesis 3).

questions.q: The mean-reverting level of Δln(PRIVt) is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because a "+" is used instead of a "–" at the denominator of the formula to obtain the mean-reverting level:
b0/(1 + b1) = 0.00259/(1 + 0.38616) = 0.0019 ≈ 0.002

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the mean-reverting level of the dependent variable of an AR(1) model is obtained as follows:
b0/(1 – b1) = 0.00259/(1 – 0.38616) = 0.0042 ≈ 0.004

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because, in the formula to calculate the mean-reverting level, b0 and b1 are swapped:
b1/(1 – b0) = 0.38616/(1 – 0.00259) = 0.3872 ≈ 0.387

questions.q: Do the estimates of the residual regression parameters indicate that the AR(1) model on Δln(PUBLt) is misspecified?
options: Yes, because there is evidence of significant serial correlation
Yes, because there is evidence of autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH)
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Residual Regression 2 indicates that the model exhibits autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH), hence it is not well specified. 
Robert E. Engle showed that we can test whether a time series is ARCH(1) by regressing the squared residuals from a previously estimated time-series model (AR, MA, or ARMA) on a constant and one lag of the squared residuals. We can estimate the linear regression equation: εt2 = a0 + a1 εt–12 + ut, where ut is an error term. If the estimate of a1 is statistically significantly different from zero, we conclude that the time series is ARCH(1).
Here, the relevant regression is Residual Regression 2 and the t-statistic for the a1 coefficient is 2.94, which is greater than the critical value of 1.97.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because there is no evidence of significant serial correlation based on Residual Regression 1. The slope coefficient of Residual Regression 1 is not statistically different from 0, which indicates that we cannot reject the null hypothesis that the residuals are not autocorrelated. An additional lag should be added to the AR model if the residuals were autocorrelated.
To decide which autoregressive model to use, take the following steps:
Estimate an AR(1) model.
Test to see whether the residuals from this model have significant serial correlation.
If you find no significant serial correlation in the residuals, you can use the AR(1) model to forecast.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because Residual Regression 2 indicates that the model exhibits autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH). Robert E. Engle showed that we can test whether a time series is ARCH(1) by regressing the squared residuals from a previously estimated time-series model (AR, MA, or ARMA) on a constant and one lag of the squared residuals. We can estimate the linear regression equation: εt2 = a0 + a1 εt–12 + ut, where ut is an error term. If the estimate of a1 is statistically significantly different from zero, we conclude that the time series is ARCH(1).
Here, the relevant regression is Residual Regression 2 and the t-statistic for the a1 coefficient is 2.94, which is greater than the critical value of 1.97.

questions.q: To perform feature selection, Silva should select the tokens with the:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because tokens with the lowest term frequency (TF) are likely to be noise features, which Silva wants to remove. Frequency measures can be used for vocabulary pruning to remove noise features by filtering the tokens with very high and low TF values across all the texts. Noisy features are both the most frequent and most sparse (or rare) tokens in the dataset. Noisy features can be sparse terms that are present in only a few text cases. The rare tokens mislead the ML model into classifying texts containing the rare terms into a specific class, an example of model overfitting. Identifying and removing noise features is very critical for text classification applications.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because Silva wants to remove noise features and select the tokens that tend to occur more often in a particular class of text, which are those with the highest mutual information (MI). Mutual information (MI) measures how much information is contributed by a token to a class of texts. The mutual information value will be equal to 0 if the token’s distribution in all text classes is the same. The MI value approaches 1 as the token in any one class tends to occur more often in only that particular class of text.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because tokens with the highest document frequency (DF) are likely to be noise features, which Silva wants to remove. Document frequency (DF) is a frequency measure that helps to discard the noise features that carry no specific information about the text class and are present across all texts. Noisy features are both the most frequent and most sparse (or rare) tokens in the dataset. Noisy features can be stop words that are typically present frequently in all the texts across the dataset. The frequent tokens strain the ML model to choose a decision boundary among the texts as the terms are present across all the texts, an example of model underfitting. Identifying and removing noise features is very critical for text classification applications.

title: Mock 1 · Denton: WestLedge ethics
body:
Michael Denton, CFA, founded WestLedge Financial, a registered investment advisory firm, five years ago. WestLedge is a small firm with just three employees. Denton is the firm's only investment professional, while the other two employees handle administrative tasks.
In a prior quarterly report to clients, Denton wrote that he had been researching artificial intelligence (AI) for over a year and believed it may improve WestLedge's existing investment process. Since distributing the client report, Denton has begun using AI to generate corporate earnings forecasts and screen securities for potential purchase in the firm's growth-oriented equity portfolios. He does not incorporate AI into the investment process for WestLedge's other equity strategies. Because AI is used only for growth-oriented portfolios, Denton does not disclose the use of AI in the firm's current quarterly client report. 
Denton is eager to expand WestLedge's business and actively encourages referrals from his professional and personal contacts. A friend of Denton's, Karri Lynch, has regularly referred clients to him over the past three years. Denton has offered to pay Lynch referral fees but she always declines, saying she is just trying to help a friend and will not accept compensation. Denton does not disclose to clients that he has offered to pay referral fees to Lynch. Each year, Denton and Lynch vacation together and Denton always pays for both of their plane tickets from his personal bank account. Denton does not disclose to clients the payments for Lynch's travel.
Denton recently accepted an unpaid position on the investment committee of XLR Corporation's pension plan. XLR is a publicly traded biotechnology company that Denton has been recommending to clients. Denton was recommended for the committee position by Martin Hunter, the CEO of XLR, who is also a client of WestLedge. Denton does not disclose to clients his appointment or that Hunter is a client of WestLedge. 
Hunter asks Denton for his opinion on Bio13, a biotechnology company that just went public. After performing appropriate due diligence, Denton recommends that Hunter buy shares of Bio13. Denton also informs Hunter that he plans to buy Bio13 shares in his own personal account but has determined that Bio13 is not suitable for any of his other clients. Hunter asks Denton to delay purchasing Bio13 shares in Hunter's account for 30 days, at which time his annual bonus will be deposited into the account. Denton immediately buys shares of Bio13 in his own account, and his purchase temporarily increases the price of the shares. Thirty days later, Denton purchases shares of Bio13 in Hunter's account.

questions.q: In his actions relating to the use of AI, does Denton comply with the Standards?
options: No, he violates the Standard relating to fair dealing
No, he violates the Standard relating to communication with clients and prospective clients
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Denton must keep clients and other interested parties informed on an ongoing basis about changes to the investment process, especially newly identified significant risks and limitations. He has failed to do this and is in violation of Standard V(B): Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions – Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Standard III(B): Duties to Clients – Fair Dealing states Members and Candidates must deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities. Denton's decision to incorporate AI for growth portfolios but not for other strategies is not a fair dealing violation. Denton is allowed to pursue different disciplines for different investment styles, changing the investment analysis process for growth-oriented portfolios while not making the same change for other equity strategies.  

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because Denton has an obligation to communicate this change in his investment process to his clients and prospective clients. Some clients might consider AI technology untested and not be comfortable with its associated risks.
Standard V(B): Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions – Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients states Members and Candidates must: 1. Disclose to clients and prospective clients the basic format and general principles of the investment processes they use to analyze investments, select securities, and construct portfolios and must promptly disclose any changes that might materially affect those processes. 2. Disclose to clients and prospective clients significant limitations and risks associated with the investment process. 
From the Guidance for Standard V(B): The member or candidate must keep clients and other interested parties informed on an ongoing basis about changes to the investment process, especially newly identified significant risks and limitations. Only by thoroughly understanding the nature of the investment product or service can a client determine whether changes to that product or service could materially affect his or her investment objectives.

questions.q: With respect to the referrals from Lynch, does Denton comply with the Standards?
options: No, because he did not disclose the payments for travel
No, because he did not disclose the offer of referral fees
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because under Standard VI(C): Conflicts of Interest – Referral Fees, Denton has an obligation to inform clients referred by Lynch of all forms of compensation provided to Lynch, including the plane tickets he purchases for her each year. Members and Candidates must disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because under Standard VI(C): Conflicts of Interest – Referral Fees, Denton has an obligation to inform clients referred by Lynch of all forms of compensation provided to Lynch, including the plane tickets he purchases for her each year. Members and Candidates must disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because there is no requirement under the Standards to disclose to clients and prospective clients an offer of referral fees that was not accepted. However, if Lynch had accepted Denton's offer and payments were made, under the Standards this would need to be disclosed to clients and prospective clients.

questions.q: With respect to the investment committee position, does Denton violate the Standards?
options: Yes, by not disclosing that Hunter is a client
Yes, by not disclosing his appointment to the committee
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Denton's appointment to the investment committee of XLR Corporation's pension plan should be disclosed to his clients and prospective clients, as his new responsibilities could create conflicts of interest.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the fact that Hunter is a client is confidential information that should not be disclosed to other clients and prospective clients. Standard III(E): Duties to Clients – Preservation of Confidentiality states Members and Candidates must keep information about current, former, and prospective clients confidential unless: 1. The information concerns illegal activities on the part of the client; 2. Disclosure is required by law; or 3. The client or prospective client permits disclosure of the information. None of these three exceptions apply in the case of Denton and Hunter. 

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because Denton's appointment to the investment committee of XLR Corporation's pension plan should be disclosed to his clients and prospective clients, as his new responsibilities could create conflicts of interest.
Standard VI(A): Conflicts of Interest – Disclosure of Conflicts states Members and Candidates must avoid or make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and employer.
From the Guidance for Standard VI(A): Service as a director (investment committee member) poses three basic conflicts of interest. First, a conflict may exist between the duties owed to clients and the duties owed to shareholders of the company. Second, investment personnel who serve as directors (investment committee members) may receive the securities or options to purchase securities of the company as compensation for serving on the board, which could raise questions about trading actions that might increase the value of those securities. Third, board service creates the opportunity to receive material nonpublic information involving the company. Even though the information is confidential, the perception could be that information not available to the public is being communicated to a director’s firm—whether a broker, investment adviser, or other type of organization.

questions.q: Did Denton comply with the Standards when purchasing Bio13 shares in his personal account?
options: No, he violated the Standard relating to market manipulation
No, he violated the Standard relating to priority of transactions
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because Denton did not violate Standard VI(B): Conflicts of Interest – Priority of Transactions, which states: Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner. Denton did not trade ahead of (front-run) his client. Hunter had previously disclosed that he would not be purchasing Bio13 for 30 days and he was not disadvantaged by Denton's trade in any way – Denton's demand for liquidity for his personal trade was temporary, and Bio13's market price 30 days later will be influenced by subsequent developments in the biotech equity market and within Bio13.  

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Denton's trade is not a form of market manipulation. Even though it temporarily moves the price of Bio13, there was no intent to mislead market participants. The market impact caused by his trade is temporary and is not a determining factor in the price Hunter will pay 30 days later.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Denton does not trade ahead of (front-run) his client. Hunter had previously disclosed that he would not be purchasing Bio13 for 30 days and he was not disadvantaged by Denton's trade in any way –the market impact caused by Denton's trade is temporary and is not a determining factor in the price Hunter will pay 30 days

title: Mock 2 · Bisht: convertible and embedded options
body:
Yuvan Bisht, a fixed-income portfolio manager, is reviewing investments in his fund.
Bisht values a convertible bond issued one year ago by Doredum at a par value of $100. Each bond can be converted to 25 shares of Doredum common stock. The current share price is $3.80. A comparable option-free bond of the same maturity is valued at $105. Based on Doredum's strong operating performance, Bisht expects its share price will reach $8.00 in one year.
Next, Bisht values a 3% default-free annual coupon bond with a 2-year maturity. The bond is putable at par ($100) at the end of Year 1. He estimates the binomial interest rate tree shown in Exhibit 1, assuming interest rate volatility of 15% and that branching from each node to a high state and to a low state occurs with equal probability.
A binomial diagram with two column heads: Year zero and Year 1. Year zero: 2 point zero zero percent. Arrow up to Year 1: 4 point 6 4 percent. Arrow down to 3 point 4 4 percent.
Expand / Collapse Extended Description
Bisht considers a scenario in which the assumed level of interest rate volatility increases from 15% to 25%. He considers the impact of this scenario on the value of the putable bond.
Bisht analyzes the effects of an interest rate scenario in which there is a non-parallel shift in the yield curve, where the only change in the curve is a 30 bp increase in the 2-year benchmark. He considers the most appropriate measure to evaluate the putable bond's sensitivity to this scenario.

questions.q: The minimum value today of the Doredum convertible bond is:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this is the conversion value of the bond. The conversion value based on the current stock price is $3.80 × 25 = $95

questions.q: Under Bisht’s volatility scenario, the value of the putable bond would most likely:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because under a scenario where interest rate volatility is assumed to be higher, the value of the putable bond increases. The value of the putable bond is the i) value of a similar straight bond plus the ii) value of the put option. Therefore, with higher interest rate volatility, the value of the put option increases, causing the overall value of the putable bond to increase and not decrease.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the value of any embedded option, regardless of the type of option, increases with interest rate volatility and hence impacts the value of the bond.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because under a scenario where interest rate volatility is assumed to be higher, the value of the putable bond increases. The value of the putable bond is the i) value of a similar straight bond plus the ii) value of the put option. Therefore, with higher interest rate volatility, the value of the put option increases, causing the overall value of the putable bond to increase.

questions.q: Based on his interest rate scenario, which of the following types of duration would be most appropriate for Bisht to use in evaluating the putable bond?
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the key rate durations reflect the sensitivity of the bond’s price to change in specific maturities on the benchmark yield curve. Thus, key rate durations help identify the ‘shaping risk’ for bonds—that is, the bond’s sensitivity to changes with the shape of the yield curve (e.g., steepening and flattening). In this case, the interest rate scenario is for a non-parallel shift in the yield curve with only the 2-year benchmark rate changing.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the effective duration indicates the sensitivity of the bond’s price to a parallel shift of the benchmark yield curve - normally calculated by averaging the changes resulting from shifting the benchmark yield curve up and down by the same amount and not change in one-specific maturity. Effective duration is less appropriate for measuring sensitivity to non-parallel shifts as in this case.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because one-sided duration is the effective duration when interest rates go up or down and are better at capturing the interest rate sensitivity of a callable or putable bond than the normal effective durations, as the upside is capped in the callable bond and down-side is capped in the putable bond. However, since the measure is based on effective duration, it is still based on a parallel shift in the yield curve and not non-parallel shift as per the case here.

title: Mock 2 · Albertson: Xita and Garc multiples
body:
David Albertson is an equity analyst at an investment bank. He is preparing updated research reports on two companies, Xita Incorporated and Garc Company.
Xita Incorporated
In Albertson's previous report on Xita, the stock had a forward P/E ratio of 14.9 and a trailing P/E ratio of 15.7. He considers a likely explanation for the difference in the P/E ratios.
Albertson indicates in his updated report that Xita's profits are cyclical. Using the data for the past four years in Exhibit 1, he computes Xita's normalized EPS based on the average ROE method. He determines that Year 1 through Year 4 (the most recent year) constitutes a full business cycle.
Exhibit 1
 	Year 1	Year 2	Year 3	Year 4
EPS	$3.19	$2.21	$0.37	$2.56
Book value per share	$10.90	$12.50	$12.60	$13.30
Garc Company
Albertson next reviews Garc, which operates in a previously mature industry that now has high growth potential due to a recent technological innovation. Garc's debt-to-equity ratio is significantly higher than the average of its competitors. Garc spent heavily on advertising to create and maintain its brand, which is an important asset. The company is favored by many investors because its dividend payout ratio is the highest in its industry. Albertson considers several potential metrics to use in valuing Garc.
During the past year, Garc's share price rose from $27.95 to $31.05 per share and the company paid an annual dividend of $1.24 per share. Over the same period, the market index rose from 550.40 to 602.21 and had an average dividend yield of 3.4%. Albertson computes Garc's relative strength compared to the index, which is a common technical indicator.

questions.q: Which of the following would best explain the difference between the two Xita P/E ratios in Albertson's previous report?
options: An estimated stock value below the current market price
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because for companies with rising earnings, the forward P/E will be smaller than the trailing P/E because the denominator in the forward P/E calculation will be larger. In the previous report, Xita had a forward P/E ratio of 14.9 and a trailing P/E ratio of 15.7, which is consistent with rising earnings at the company.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because with the numerator (current stock price) being the same in both ratios, any difference between the trailing and forward P/E ratios must arise from differences in earnings per share. Any expected increase in earnings, even if positive growth was slower than forecast, will result in a forward P/E less than the trailing P/E.
If the earnings growth forecast was negative, the forward P/E would be greater, not smaller (as in the vignette), as the forward P/E denominator would be smaller than the trailing P/E denominator.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the numerator (current stock price) is the same in both the trailing and forward P/E ratios.

questions.q: Xita's normalized EPS based on the average ROE method is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this is computed as the average EPS for Years 1 to 4:
(3.19 + 2.21 + 0.37 + 2.56)/4 = $2.08

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this is the average ROE for Years 1 to 4 (17.28%) multiplied by the average BVPS for Years 1 to 4 ($12.325, calculated as [10.90 + 12.50 + 12.60 + 13.30 ]/4):
0.1728 × 12.325 = $2.13

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because in the method of average return on equity normalized EPS is calculated as the average return on equity (ROE) from the most recent full cycle, multiplied by current book value per share.
Each year's ROE is computed by dividing EPS by BVPS, giving ROE values, by year, of:
Year 1: 3.19/10.90 = 29.3%
Year 2: 2.21/12.50 =17.7%
Year 3: 0.37/12.60 = 2.9%
Year 4: 2.56/13.30 =19.2%
The average ROE for Years 1 to 4 is (29.3 + 17.7 + 2.9 + 19.2)]/4 = 17.28%. Multiplying this by the current BVPS ($13.30 in Year 4) results in normalized EPS of $2.30.

questions.q: Which of the following is the most appropriate metric for Albertson to use in valuing Garc?
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect as dividend yield is only one component of total return; not using all information related to expected return is suboptimal. With growth opportunities arising in the industry, capital gains are likely to be an important source of future returns.
In addition, the investment required to capitalize on the growth opportunities may adversely affect Garc's ability to pay dividends in the future – especially because Garc's dividend payout ratio is the highest in the industry, which is attractive to many of its current investors. A useful metric in assessing the safety of the dividend is the payout ratio: A high payout relative to other companies operating in the same industry may indicate a less secure dividend because the dividend is less well covered by earnings.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect as a material portion of Garc's value arises from the value of its brand, which as an internally generated intangible asset is not shown on the balance sheet (and thus not reflected in book value per share).
Assets in addition to those recognized in financial statements may be critical operating factors. For example, in many service companies, human capital—the value of skills and knowledge possessed by the workforce—is more important than physical capital as an operating factor, but it is not reflected as an asset on the balance sheet.
In addition, accounting effects on book value may compromise how useful book value is as a measure of the shareholders’ investment in the company. In general, intangible assets that are generated internally (as opposed to being acquired) are not shown as assets on a company’s balance sheet. For example, companies account for advertising and marketing as expenses, so the value of internally generated brands, which are created and maintained by advertising and marketing activities, do not appear as assets on a company’s balance sheet under IFRS or US GAAP.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the numerator of the EV/Sales ratio is the firm's total value of debt and equity. EV/S is an alternative sales-based ratio that is particularly useful when comparing companies with diverse capital structures, which applies to Garc's industry. Sales is an appropriate denominator as sales growth is consistent and not as variable as earnings. In addition, sales are generally less subject to distortion or manipulation than are other fundamentals, such as EPS or book value.

questions.q: Garc's relative strength compared to the market index over the past year is closest to:
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the relative strength measure of Garc against the market index is 1.0154.
The value of Garc divided by the index at the beginning of the period is 27.95 / 550.40 = 0.050781; the relative strength on that day is thus 0.050781 / 0.050781 = 1.0000.
At the end of the time frame, the value of Garc divided by the index is 31.05 / 602.21 = 0.051560. Thus, over the time frame the relative strength measure for Garc is 0.051560 / 0.050781 = 1.0153.
Dividends are not incorporated into the relative strength calculation because relative strength is based strictly on price movement. Also, the valuation indicators we call momentum indicators relate either price or a fundamental, such as earnings, to the time series of their own past values.
A simple relative-strength indicator of the second type (i.e., the stock’s performance relative to the performance of some group of stocks) is the stock’s performance divided by the performance of an equity index. If the value of this ratio increases, the stock price increases relative to the index and displays positive relative strength.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this is 1 plus the Garc price return of 11.09% (31.05 / 27.95 – 1) minus the market index price return of 9.41% (602.21 / 550.40 – 1):
1 + 11.09% – 9.41% = 1.0168

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this is the total return including dividends:
Garc total return = Price return + Dividend return = 31.05/27.95 + 1.24/27.95 = 1.155277
Index total return: Price return + Dividend return = (602.21/550.40) + 3.4% = 1.094131 + 0.034 = 1.128131
Return ratio: 1.155277 / 1.128131 = 1.0241

title: Mock 2 · Edberg: Alfa dividends and board
body:
Greta Edberg is an activist investor with Sintra Partners. Sintra recently acquired a 9.9% equity position in Alfa Corporation and is seeking two board seats. 
Alfa is a mature company that has maintained a constant dividend payout ratio and does not currently have a share repurchase program. In public comments, Edberg recommends a material increase in Alfa's dividend payout ratio and benchmarking the payout to Alfa's competitors.
Edberg tells Alfa's management that Minskar, one of Alfa's competitors, has a 75% target payout ratio with an adjustment period of four years. Minskar's most recent annual dividend was $0.25 per share. Minskar's EPS is expected to be $1.30 in Year 1 and $1.10 in Year 2 of the adjustment period.
As an alternative to Alfa increasing dividends, Edberg proposes a one-time share repurchase using borrowed funds. Edberg's current EPS forecast for Alfa for the next year is $1.50. The company currently has 2,267,000 shares outstanding, its current share price is $30, and its after-tax cost of borrowing is 4.25%. Edberg calculates the revised EPS forecast for Alfa, assuming that 250,000 shares are repurchased immediately at the current share price.
Taylor Greene, an analyst, oversees the integration of ESG factors into Sintra's investment analysis. Greene analyzes current policies and practices related to Alfa's board and recommends changes that would increase governance effectiveness. Alfa's board has 13 members, seven of whom are independent, and is chaired by the company's CEO. The board has audit, compensation, nomination, risk and compliance, and governance committees.

questions.q: The implementation of Edberg's recommendation regarding Alfa's dividend payout ratio would most likely:
options: reduce management's ability to invest in negative NPV projects.
increase the agency conflict between Alfa's managers and shareholders.
reduce the agency conflict between Alfa's bondholders and shareholders.
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because increasing the dividend payout ratio (i.e., paying out a higher percentage of earnings as dividends) would constrain Alfa management's access to capital, and thus their ability to overinvest by taking on negative NPV projects. One managerial incentive of particular concern is the potential private benefit managers may obtain from investment in negative net present value (NPV) projects. Such projects will generate negative economic returns; but because they may grow the size of the company (measured in sales or assets) and thus enlarge the manager’s span of control, the manager may have the incentive to invest in them. The potential overinvestment agency problem might be alleviated by the payment of dividends. In particular, by paying out all free cash flow to equity in dividends, managers would be constrained in their ability to overinvest by taking on negative NPV projects.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because increasing the dividend payout ratio would reduce, rather than increase, the agency conflict between managers and shareholders. As a mature company, paying out more dividends would dissuade managers from overinvesting in negative NPV projects.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because increasing the dividend payout ratio would increase, not reduce, the agency conflict between Alfa's bondholders and shareholders. Another concern when a company is financed by debt as well as equity is that paying dividends can exacerbate the agency conflict between shareholders and bondholders. When a company has debt outstanding, the payment of dividends reduces the cash cushion available to the company for the disbursement of fixed required payments to bondholders.

questions.q: Using a target payout adjustment model, the expected increase in Minskar's dividend per share in Year 2 of the adjustment period is closest to:
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the expected increase in dividends = (Expected earnings × Target payout ratio − Previous dividend) × Adjustment factor. The expected dividend increases for Minskar are as follows:
In Year 1: ($1.30 × 0.75 − $0.25) × 0.25 = $0.18125 (for a Year 1 dividend of $0.43125)
In Year 2: ($1.10 × 0.75 − $0.43125) × 0.25 = $0.0984375 ≈ $0.10

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the calculation uses a 100% target payout ratio instead of 75%, as follows:
In Year 1: ($1.30 × 1.00 − $0.25) × 0.25 = $0.2625 (for a Year 1 dividend of $0.5125)
In Year 2: ($1.10 × 1.00 − $0.5125) × 0.25 = $0.146875 ≈ $0.15

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this is the expected Year 1 increase, as follows:
In Year 1: ($1.30 × 0.75 − $0.25) × 0.25 = $0.18125 ≈ $0.18

questions.q: If the proposed share repurchase is implemented immediately, Edberg's revised EPS forecast for Alfa for the next year would be closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this calculation does not adjust for the new share count in the EPS calculation:
($3,400,500 − $318,750) / 2,267,000 shares
= $3,081,750 / 2,267,000 shares
≈ $1.36

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because EPS after the share repurchase is calculated as follows:
Earnings = EPS x Number of shares = $1.50 x 2,267,000 = $3,400,500
Funds needed to repurchase shares = $30 x 250,000 = $7,500,000
Cost of funds to repurchase shares = 4.25% x $7,500,000 = $318,750
Number of shares after repurchase = 2,267,000 − 250,000 = 2,017,000
Using the above information, we have:
EPS after buyback = (Earnings − After-tax cost of funds) / Shares outstanding after buyback
= [$3,400,500 − ($7,500,000 × 0.0425)] / 2,017,000 shares
= ($3,400,500 − $318,750) / 2,017,000 shares
= $3,081,750 / 2,017,000 shares
≈ $1.53

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this answer choice does not consider the cost of borrowing in the EPS calculation:
($3,400,500 − $0) / 2,017,000 shares
= $3,400,500 / 2,017,000 shares
≈ $1.69

questions.q: Which of the following characteristics of Alfa's board is most likely to pose the greatest potential governance concern?
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because Alfa's CEO also serves as board chair, which is not a characteristic of effective corporate governance.
Generally, when evaluating board structure, investors consider whether the organization and structure of the board provide sufficient oversight, representation, and accountability to shareholders. A related topic is 'CEO duality,' whereby the chief executive officer (CEO) also serves as chairperson of the board. CEO duality may raise concerns that the monitoring and oversight role of the board may be compromised relative to independent chairperson and CEO roles. When the chairperson is not independent or the role is combined, a company may appoint a lead independent director to help protect investor interests.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Alfa has a comprehensive set of board committees. The number of board committees and how the committees operate are relevant considerations in an investor’s analysis of governance. Committees vary by corporation and industry but generally include audit, governance, remuneration (or compensation), nomination, and risk and compliance committees.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because 7 of the 13 directors (54%) on Alfa's board are independent. The independence of the directors is a relevant consideration for investors. The absence or presence of a minority of independent directors is a negative aspect of corporate governance. Without independent directors, the potential exists for management to act in a self-serving manner. Consequently, a lack of independent directors on a board may increase investors’ perception of the corporation’s risk.

title: Mock 2 · Nicola: VaR and backtesting
body:
Adriani Nicola is an analyst for an investment consulting firm. She is preparing an analysis of equity funds for an institutional client.
Nicola evaluates risk metrics for the Lagunas Fund. For her current analysis, Nicola calculates a 5% daily VaR using the parametric method. Lagunas has $175 million in assets under management and is expected to have an annual return of 8.80% with a standard deviation of 14.25%. She assumes 250 trading days in a year. In a standard normal distribution, a 5% VaR is 1.65 standard deviations below the expected value. 
Nicola supplements her analysis with an annual﻿﻿﻿﻿ 5% VaR using the historical simulation approach over a 10-year period. She observes higher volatility in recent years, which she expects to persist in the future. Nicola is concerned that VaR using the historical simulation approach may not adequately reflect the higher volatility and considers potential revisions to this approach.
The Lagunas Fund has a large position in ABC stock, whose price has been extremely volatile. The portfolio manager has proposed reducing the fund's position in ABC stock by 3%. Nicola considers a measure to capture how the VaR of the fund would change if the reduction was implemented.
Nicola evaluates three multifactor equity strategies that use a risk parity approach to portfolio construction. Each strategy's investment objective is to achieve market returns with potential for upside, while managing volatility and extreme downside risk. As part of her evaluation, Nicola backtests the three strategies using monthly returns from the past 20 years. She assesses the backtest results shown in Exhibit 1.
Exhibit 1
 	Mean Return	Maximum Return	Minimum Return	Standard Deviation	Skewness	Kurtosis
Strategy A	0.71%	3.60%	–2.40%	1.46%	0.15	8.70
Strategy B	0.68%	3.40%	–2.30%	1.39%	–0.25	6.50
Strategy C	0.70%	3.50%	–2.35%	1.44%	0.65	4.20

questions.q: In Nicola's current analysis, the 5% daily parametric VaR for the Lagunas Fund is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this calculation uses a critical value of 1 instead of 1.65 (or, effectively omits the critical value).
Step 1: Multiply the portfolio standard deviation by 1.00: 0.00901249 × 1.00 = 0.00901249
Step 2: Subtract the answer obtained in Step 1 from the expected return: 0.000352 − 0.00901249 = −0.00866049
Step 3: Because VaR is expressed as an absolute number (despite representing an expected loss), change the sign of the value obtained in Step 2 to 0.00866049
Step 4: Multiply the result from Step 3 by the value of the portfolio: $175,000,000 × 0.00866049 = $1,515,586 ≈ $1.52 million.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the 5% daily parametric VaR is calculated as follows:
First, convert the portfolio annual return and standard deviation to daily figures: Portfolio return = 0.0880/250 = 0.000352
Portfolio standard deviation = 0.1425/√(250) = 0.00901249
The following step-by-step procedure shows how VaR is derived:
Step 1: Multiply the portfolio standard deviation by 1.65: 0.00901249 × 1.65 = 0.01487061
Step 2: Subtract the answer obtained in Step 1 from the expected return: 0.000352 − 0.01487061 = −0.01451861
Step 3: Because VaR is expressed as an absolute number (despite representing an expected loss), change the sign of the value obtained in Step 2 to 0.01451861
Step 4: Multiply the result from Step 3 by the value of the portfolio: $175,000,000 × 0.01451861 = $2,540,757 ≈ $2.54 million.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the calculation adds, rather than subtracts, the product of the critical value and the standard deviation.
Step 1: Multiply the portfolio standard deviation by 1.65: 0.00901249 × 1.65 = 0.01487061
Step 2: (Incorrect) Add the answer obtained in Step 1 to the expected return: 0.000352 + 0.01487061 = 0.01522261
Step 3: Because VaR is expressed as an absolute number (despite representing an expected loss), change the sign of the value obtained in Step 2 to 0.01522261
Step 4: Multiply the result from Step 3 by the value of the portfolio: $175,000,000 × 0.01522261 = $2,663,957 ≈ $2.66 million.

questions.q: Given Nicola's volatility expectation, the most appropriate revision when supplementing her analysis with an annual 5% VAR would be to:
options: assume a normal distribution of returns.
increase the weight of more recent observations.
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because using a wider confidence interval would increase the confidence level (e.g., from 95% to 99%) and produce a larger VaR estimate, but would not directly incorporate Nicola's volatility view.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because, although the historical simulation approach is not constrained by an assumption of normality, assuming a normal distribution in this case would not incorporate Nicola's expectation of recent higher volatility persisting into the future.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because both the parametric and historical simulation methods in their most basic forms have the limitation that, as with most samples, all observations are weighted equally. The historical simulation method can adjust for this problem, however, by using a weighting methodology that gives more weight to more recent observations and less weight to more distant observations.

questions.q: Which of the following would best capture the effect on the Lagunas Fund's VaR of the proposed reduction in the ABC stock position?
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because relative VaR is a measure of the degree to which the performance of a given investment portfolio might deviate from its benchmark. It does not capture how portfolio VaR will change if a position size is changed relative to the remaining positions.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because conditional VaR is the average loss conditional on exceeding VaR cutoff. It does not capture how portfolio VaR will change if a position size is changed relative to the remaining positions.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because incremental VaR measures how the portfolio VaR will change if a position size is changed relative to the remaining positions suppose the portfolio manager is contemplating increasing the risk by increasing the investment in SPY to 90% of the portfolio. We recalculate the VaR under the proposed allocation, and the incremental VaR is the difference between the 'before' and 'after' VaR. The potential 3% change in the ABC stock position is exactly the type of change incremental VaR is intended to measure.

questions.q: Based on the backtest results, the multifactor equity strategy that best achieves the investment objective is:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Strategy A has similar returns and volatility to those of Strategy C, but has a lower probability of positive returns (lower positive skewness) and is more fat-tailed (higher kurtosis, which can lead to extreme negative surprises).

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Strategy B has similar returns and volatility to those of Strategy C, but has a lower probability of positive returns (negative skewness) and is more fat-tailed (higher kurtosis, which can lead to extreme negative surprises).

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the backtest results for Strategy C best meet the objective to achieve market returns with potential for upside, while managing volatility and extreme downside risk. Strategy C has similar returns and volatility to those of Strategy A and Strategy B, but has a higher probability of positive returns (higher positive skewness) and is less fat-tailed (lower kurtosis).

title: Mock 2 · Bernard: currency arbitrage and carry
body:
Joanne Bernard is a currency trader for a US-based hedge fund. She reviews interbank bid-offer quotes in Exhibit 1 (USD/EUR is the number of USD per 1 EUR; JPY/USD is the number of JPY per 1 USD). Bernard determines if an arbitrage profit is possible for the fund based on a dealer's bid/offer rate quote of 119.38/119.40 in JPY/EUR. 
Exhibit 1
Currency Pair	Interbank Bid	Interbank Offer
USD/EUR	1.1416	1.1421
JPY/USD	104.62	104.68
The hedge fund considers hedging a New Zealand dollar (NZD) 1,000,000 coupon payment it will receive in six months. Bernard calculates the 6-month forward USD/NZD (number of USD per 1 NZD) exchange rate implied by covered interest rate parity. Note that MRR is the market reference rate.
6-month annualized MRR in the US is 0.50%
6-month annualized MRR in New Zealand is 1.00%
The spot mid-market currency quote for USD/NZD is 0.6808
Bernard next considers a 1-year carry trade that involves borrowing the USD and investing in the Brazilian real (BRL). She computes the all-in return (measured in USD terms) of the carry trade using the following information:
Spot mid-market quote for the BRL/USD is 5.1300
1-year MRR in the US is 1.00%
1-year MRR in Brazil is 9.75%
The BRL/USD exchange rate in one year is 5.2000
Finally, Bernard is concerned about a currency crisis in emerging market Country B. She notes the following conditions about the country:
Condition 1: A slight decline of foreign investment in its equity market
Condition 2: Broad money growth and a decline in the ratio of M2 (a measure of money supply) to bank reserves 
Condition 3: A sizable decline in the ratio of foreign exchange (FX) reserve holdings to average daily FX turnover in their domestic currency

questions.q: Based on the dealer's JPY/EUR quote, is there an arbitrage opportunity for the hedge fund?
options: Yes, by purchasing EUR in the interbank market and selling EUR to the dealer
Yes, by purchasing EUR from the dealer and selling EUR in the interbank market
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because there is an arbitrage opportunity by buying EUR from the dealer and selling in the interbank market.   

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the arbitrage opportunity is the opposite of this transaction, as explained in the response rationale for the correct answer. The fund should buy EUR from the dealer and sell it in the interbank market. 

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the dealer's quote of JPY/EUR 119.38/119.40 leads to arbitrage as follows:
In the interbank market we have the following rates from Exhibit 1:
 	Bid	Offer
1. USD/EUR	1.1416	1.1421
2. JPY/USD	104.62	104.68
3. Implied JPY/EUR (1 × 2)	119.4342	119.5550
4. DEALER (info in vignette)	119.38	119.40
 
Therefore, the hedge fund can buy EUR from the dealer at JPY119.40 (row 4) and then effectively sell EUR in the interbank market for 119.43 (from row 3).

questions.q: Based on covered interest rate parity, the 6-month forward USD/NZD exchange rate is closest to:
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the annual interest rates are used rather than the correct 6-month interest rates as follows (where S0 is the spot exchange rate expressed as USD/NZD)
F(USD/NZD) = S0 × (1+rUS)/(1+rNZD) = 0.6808 × (1.005)/(1+0.01) = 0.6774

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the 6-month forward rate is calculated using the correct formula and interest rates for the covered interest rate parity forward rate (S0 is the current spot exchange rate which is equal to 0.6808).
Ff/d = Sf/d × [1 + if(actual/360)]/[1 + id(Actual/360)]
F(USD/NZD) = S0 × (1+rUS/2)/(1+rNZD/2) = 0.6808 × (1 + 0.005/2)/(1+0.01/2) = 0.6791

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because the ratio of interest rates is inverted as follows:
F(USD/NZD) = S0 × (1+rNZD/2)/(1+rUS/2) = 0.6808 × (1 + 0.01/2)/(1+0.005/2) = 0.6825

questions.q: The all-in return for the carry trade, measured in USD terms, is closest to:
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because it considers both the return from the BRL investment and then also deducts the cost of borrowing USD. We can see this as follows for borrowing a hypothetical USD1,000 as follows:
Borrow $1,000 at 1% for 1 year, end of year value $1,010
Convert to BRL at 5.130; this becomes BRL 5,130
Invest BRL 5,130 at the Brazilian rate of 9.75% for 1 year.
The investment in (3) becomes BRL 5,130 × 1.0975 = BRL 5,630.175
Convert at the t=1 year exchange rate of BRL 5.200 which gives USD 1,082.72596
Pay back the borrowing from (1): USD 1,010.00
Net return in USD is the difference between (5) and (6) or USD 72.72596
Expressed in percentage USD term the amount in (7) is 0.072725 or 7.27%

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it is the rate earned on the carry trade that does not include the cost of borrowing USD. This is seen as follows for borrowing a hypothetical USD1,000:
Borrow $1,000 at 1% for 1 year, end of year value $1,010
Convert to BRL at 5.130; this becomes BRL 5,130
Invest BRL 5,130 at the Brazilian rate of 9.75% for 1 year.
The investment in (3) becomes BRL 5,130 × 1.0975 = BRL 5,630.175
Convert at the t=1 year exchange rate of BRL 5.200 which gives USD 1,082.72596
Incorrect net return, deduct $1,000 original cost USD 82.7256
As a percentage of original USD borrowed: 8.27%

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it is the interest rate differential between BRL and USD (i.e., 9.75% and 1.00%).

questions.q: Which of the following conditions would most likely be a warning sign of a currency crisis in Country B?
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it is typically large inflows of foreign capital that precede a crisis. In the vignette it is stated that Country B has experienced a slight decline in the allocation by foreign investors. 

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because studies have shown that broad money growth and the ratio of M2 (a measure of money supply) to bank reserves tend to rise prior to a currency crisis. Bernard notes that these indicators have declined.  

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because foreign exchange reserves tend to decline precipitously as a crisis approaches. In the vignette, Bernard notes that this is indeed the situation for Country B.

title: Mock 2 · Traske: insurers and banks
body:
Susan Traske is an analyst specializing in financial institutions. She is evaluating Sigmar, a large US-based commercial bank. Traske uses the CAMELS (capital adequacy, asset quality, management, earnings, liquidity, and sensitivity) approach in her evaluation of Sigmar. As part of this analysis, she examines Sigmar's liquidity ratios and notes that the bank's net stable funding ratio has increased steadily over the past three years. She then investigates which components of the ratio explain this trend.
Traske reviews Sigmar's employee compensation policy and notes that a large restricted stock grant vested during the current year. The share price on the settlement date was greater than the share price on the grant date. Recognizing that Sigmar prepares its financial statements in accordance with US GAAP, Traske considers the effect of the vested grant on Sigmar's income tax expense for the current year.
Sigmar sponsors a defined benefit pension plan for employees. Sigmar's pension disclosure for the most recent year is shown in Exhibit 1 (amounts in $ millions):
Exhibit 1
Interest cost	2,875
Current service cost	535
Actual return on plan assets	2,895
Expected return on plan assets	3,000
Traske notes that there was no amortization of past service costs, no amortization of actuarial gains or losses, and no amortization of differences between actual and expected return on plan assets.
Finally, Traske compares the overall efficiency of the underwriting operations of three property and casualty insurance companies based on the information in Exhibit 2.
Exhibit 2
 	Insurer A	Insurer B	Insurer C
Loss and loss adjustment ratio	60.2%	66.4%	63.1%
Underwriting expense ratio	42.3%	30.8%	32.5%

questions.q: An increase in which of the following would best explain the trend in Sigmar's net stable funding ratio?
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because an increase in loans to customers (a component of the bank's asset base) would be consistent with a decrease, not an increase, in the NSFR.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) is expressed as the minimum percentage of a bank’s required stable funding that must be sourced from available stable funding. For this ratio, required stable funding (the denominator) is a function of the composition and maturity of a bank’s asset base, whereas available stable funding (the numerator) is a function of the composition and maturity of a bank’s funding sources (i.e., capital and deposits and other liabilities). The NSFR has steadily increased over the past three years. Accordingly, an increase in long-term debt liabilities (a funding source) would be consistent with an increase in the NSFR.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because highly liquid assets do not enter the calculation of the Net Stable Funding Ratio.

questions.q: The difference in share price between the grant date and the settlement date for the large restricted stock grant will most likely:
options: have no effect on income tax expense.
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because a higher share price at settlement versus the grant date results in a higher tax deduction than the cumulative stock-based compensation expense. This is known as an excess tax benefit or tax windfall because taxable income and tax expense are reduced.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Sigmar follows US GAAP, so a difference in share price between the settlement date and the grant date will cause income tax expense to increase or decrease.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because a lower (not higher) share price at settlement versus at the grant date results in a lower tax deduction than the cumulative stock-based compensation expense.

questions.q: The total pension expense (in $ millions) reported on Sigmar's income statement for the most recent year is:
questions.why:
Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because there is no amortization of past service costs or actuarial gains and losses, hence the total pension expense (in $ millions) is computed as: Current service cost + Interest cost – Expected return on plan assets = 535 + 2,875 – 3,000 = 410.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this answer uses the actual (instead of expected) return on plan assets, hence the total pension expense (in $ millions) is incorrectly computed as: 535 + 2,875 – 2,895 = 515.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because this answer is the current service cost, and it ignores the interest cost and expected return on plan assets. The current service cost would be recognized in operating expense, but would not be the only pension expense reported on Sigmar's income statement for the most recent year.

questions.q: Which insurer's underwriting operation is the most efficient overall?
questions.why:
Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Insurer A has the highest combined ratio (60.2% + 42.3% = 102.5%) compared to Insurer B (66.4% + 30.8% = 97.2%) and Insurer C (63.1% + 32.5% = 95.6%), thus it does not have the most efficient underwriting operation overall.

Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Insurer B has a higher combined ratio (66.4% + 30.8% = 97.2%) than Insurer C (63.1% + 32.5% = 95.6%), thus it does not have the most efficient underwriting operation overall.

Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because Insurer C has the lowest combined ratio (63.1% + 32.5% = 95.6%) compared to Insurer A (60.2% + 42.3% = 102.5%) and Insurer B (66.4% + 30.8% = 97.2%). Combined ratio = Loss and loss adjustment expense ratio + Underwriting expense ratio. This ratio indicates the overall efficiency of an underwriting operation. A combined ratio of less than 100% is considered efficient.

title: Mock 2 · Bueden: equity swap
body:
Maximilian Bueden manages the equity exposure for a family office. All of the office's investment returns are measured in EUR, while equity holdings in foreign currencies are usually hedged to eliminate exchange rate risk. Six months ago, Bueden entered a 3-year receive-equity, pay-fixed, annual-reset equity swap with a notional amount of EUR 1,000,000. At initiation, the fixed rate was 2.3% and the equity index was trading at 100. Now the fixed rate has declined to 1.8% and the equity index is trading at 104.8.
